I never knew Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, nor did I ever have the occasion to approach him.

Only now and then, in the Vatican Basilica, during solemn ceremonies, was I able, among the other Eminences, to rest my gaze upon the venerable figure of the Cardinal Dean, the purest glory of our Naples.

I read of him in «L’Osservatore Romano» the devout addresses of homage and good wishes which, at the Christmas festivities, he offered to the Holy Father in the name of the Sacred College. In them the elegance of expression was always in harmony with the loftiness and spontaneity of feeling.

Another, therefore, with greater competence, born of happy contacts with the venerated Person of the illustrious Departed, might have written the preface to these biographical pages, few in number but simple and clear, owed to the facile pen of Fr. Ilario da Teano, Capuchin.

I could not, however, withstand the affectionate insistence of the Author, who wished to grant the poor Bishop of his Diocese, for long periods the field of his apostolic labors, the honor of a word of introduction to the Life of the Eminent Purple-robed prelate, who was for more than thirty years Cardinal Protector of the Order of Capuchin Friars.

And I must be not a little grateful to the dear Father, who has given me the opportunity to know more closely so noble and edifying a figure of a Prince of the Holy Roman Church. Having to carry out the task, I examined the pages of the biography beforehand and was able to admire the long, intelligent and industrious activity carried out by the distinguished Cardinal in the various fields of the apostolate and in high offices, to which he was called by the loving trust of no fewer than five Popes, from Leo XIII to Pius XII, happily reigning.

Because of the affectionate esteem and the immense devotion with which he was constantly surrounded, by eminent men and by the people, his person, noble by descent and by manner, deserved the honor of a biography, since without it his merits and his virtues might, with the passing of time, have fallen into oblivion.

Great, therefore, is the merit of Fr. Ilario, already known for other valuable publications, in making more widely known, with this new work, a most edifying priestly life; a soul of exceptional goodness, wholly dedicated to the Lord; a heart that knew surges of seraphic ardor and beatings of flowering and heroic charity; a strong and decisive character, wholly consecrated, in happy and in adverse times, to the cause of God, of the Church, of souls.

The pages of Fr. Ilario, while they bring into just light the innumerable merits acquired over the long years of his life by the illustrious Prince of the Holy Roman Church, reveal the extraordinary and uncommon richness of his interior life. Reading them provides tasty and solid nourishment for the spirit, and sure guidance and powerful stimulus for those who sincerely wish to make their own lives precious in the sight of God and fruitful in beneficial results for men, in the humble and wise use of the gifts of intelligence, of heart and of works.

Not everything — the Author notes on p. 55 — has been possible, because of the nearness of the times, to say and to gather about the eminent Man; especially about his work as Representative of the Holy See, as Nuncio in Vienna. This took place in a particularly difficult and delicate period, during which he had to render outstanding services to the Apostolic See, with an attitude dictated by undoubted loyalty, by irreproachable rectitude and by the sole concern to defend, against every undue interference or dangerous deviation, the inalienable rights of the Church and of souls. Such conduct earned him, shortly afterwards, from Saint Pius X, the honor of the Roman Purple.

We would therefore wish that, this first edition being soon exhausted, the pen of Fr. Ilario or of others may, on the basis of new documents, give us a fuller and more complete biography of the most pious Cardinal; whose life, bound up with a historical period of the Church of exceptional importance, was so happily summed up by His Eminence Cardinal Tappouni: «In short, I can sum up by saying: in the Prince and in the Cardinal one saw above all the priest, hard-working, pious, humble and charitable.»

And of these priestly souls, who adorn the garden of the Church of Christ, the world has always had, and has, such great need.

Teano, 18 January, Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, 1957.

† Matteo G. Sperandeo

Bishop of Calvi and Teano

Count Don Gennaro del Balzo di Presenzano, of happy memory, a deeply religious soul, had around 1913 an estate not far from the Capuchin friary of Tora (Caserta), where I was living.

For reasons of ministry I became his friend, and the friend of the whole family.

The son who has remained most attached to me is Duke Dr. Raimondo.

One day, when I was in Rome, he asked me by telephone to come to his office in Via Condotti, 68, because he had something important to tell me. I granted his wish. The next day I went to Via Condotti, and he received me kindly at once in his office; after the usual greetings he said to me: «I would like to ask you, dear Father Ilario, to write the life of my uncle the Cardinal, Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte: he was a truly pious Priest, and I wish him to be known by men and imitated.»

Without thinking of the difficulties I would meet in writing such a biography, I answered him: yes. I do not hide how much trepidation I felt, and still feel in my soul, for having pronounced that yes.

Nobody has written about Cardinal di Belmonte; there is a profile in the «MEMORIES», news and documents of the Granito family, gathered and arranged for family use, but it is laconic, very laconic. News is found here and there in newspapers and periodicals, and at times it is imprecise.

This Most Eminent Cardinal wrote no book, no work; often from works one can know the man; this source is lacking.

Don Gennaro was a Priest of intense interior virtue; God had poured into his heart gleams of supernatural light; his soul was a holy tabernacle, where grace found a luminous dwelling; he always had at his side, throughout his long apostolate, humility, the fundamental basis of true glory. He was noble with everyone, witty and cheerful with everyone, but strict and prudent in his expressions and in his manifestations. He was a man who loved uprightness, always cheerful, sociable, but extremely reserved.

While he was Nuncio in Vienna he met terrible obstacles in the person of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Count Ludwig Lex von Aehrenthal, who tried by every means to make him return to Italy, but did not succeed: Don Gennaro remained at his post, because so the Pontiff willed.

We know few things of the clashes that arose between the Count and the Nuncio. Posterity will know them.

To work on a man who covered all his activities with a profound silence, who in the depths of his heart thought only of serving God with scrupulous fidelity, is a difficult thing. The profound historian of Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte is still far from us. Certainly he will appear, but one must give time to time.

The news we publish in this little volume about the venerable Cardinal we have learned from the little that the press has handed down to us and from most respectable persons who were close to him by reason of office and of blood.

Duke Raimondo del Balzo, great-nephew of Cardinal Granito, has supplied me with a great part of the information concerning this biography.

The distinguished writer Piero Bargellini, in the preface to the life of Canon Giuseppe Allamano, founder of the Consolata Missionary Fathers and Sisters, compiled by Giovanni Barra, writes: «the literary technique used by Barra in his book is that of inlay, because, having to outline and complete the wholly spiritual figure of a master of piety, he has gathered as many gems and precious stones as he could from books of spirituality, of asceticism and of mysticism, arranging them so as to reflect and illuminate the supernatural virtues of the father of the missionaries».

If not in everything, in part it is also the technique of this work.

Don Gennaro di Belmonte, Prince of the Holy Roman Church, athlete of Christ, tireless worker in his mystical vineyard, from heaven bless this modest volume, whose purpose is to make known his long life, all light, all purity, filled with wonderful virtues, and move readers to learn in his school to keep their thoughts always turned to God, amid the harsh struggles of the world, so as to enjoy one day his ineffable joys in the immortal homeland.

Fr. Ilario da Teano

Naples is the city of songs, of enchantments, the city where mother nature has lavished her most eloquent smiles. The poet greeted her as the «Empire of harmony».

She lies majestic on one of the loveliest gulfs in the world, which takes its name from her. On the left she has Vesuvius, on the right Posillipo and the Phlegraean Fields, opposite Castellammare di Stabia, Sorrento, Capri, Ischia, Procida.

In this city, because of its extraordinary natural beauty, the ancients placed the home of the Sirens. In Naples the poet Virgil composed a great part of his works and ended his laborious day. This delightful place was dear to the emperors and to the Roman patricians; Lucullus built himself a superb villa there.

Naples has interesting museums: the National Museum is famous, with its classical statues, bronzes, mosaics and paintings from the excavations of Herculaneum and Pompeii.

The museum of Capodimonte is also important, where one admires the finest eighteenth-century porcelains from the San Martino factory and the marvellous paintings of the seventeenth-century Neapolitan school.

Leopardi loved the city of Naples greatly and met his death in it. For its history, for its University, founded by Frederick II in 1224, for the sweetness of its climate, for its ever-flowering shores, it is a longed-for destination of tourists from all over the world. Who does not know Naples through its songs, original, rich in every feeling?

It is the land of Genius, the land of Art. Homeland of Giovanni Lorenzo Bernini, of Salvator Rosa, of Luca Giordano, of the great philosopher Giovan Battista Vico.

But above all, beautiful Parthenope is the homeland of Saints. For brevity I like to recall here only Saint Alphonsus Mary de’ Liguori. How many greatnesses in this Priest! «He was wholly seraphic in ardor», like the Poor Man of Assisi; he was like Saint Francis, poet of God and of nature; he imitated the Seraphic Saint in the marvellous field of the apostolate.

The writer Mgr. Emilio Federici, in the life of Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza, notes: «To Naples belongs a fine primacy — never attained by others — that of counting the preponderant number of causes, ancient, recent, very recent, of servants of God on the way to the glory of the altars. Without saying anything of its already so well-known Saints, there are fully 50 Causes now registered at the S. Congregation of Rites bearing the customary title «Neapolitana».

Some of these servants of God, it is true, are not natives of Naples, but they lived immersed in that warm and singing atmosphere which one would think fatal to many, and which for them, on the contrary, was a means of ascent towards the heights of Holiness.

And amid the beauties of Naples was born Cardinal GENNARO GRANITO PIGNATELLI di Belmonte. He received from nature a soul that loved the beautiful, the good, the true, and above all a great passion for the Redeemer of peoples and for the Religion He founded. An upright, irreproachable Priest. During his long life he never boasted of his nobility; he was humble in the deepest sense of the word. He gave to the Sacred Purple he wore dignity and splendor. The Roman Pontiff was for him «the sweet Christ on earth», and he loved him with a transcendent love. There was no solemn and arduous circumstance in which his zeal for the rights of God and of the Church did not show itself.

The most salient feature of Cardinal di Belmonte was his love for the poor; he felt infinite tenderness for them, and died in the greatest poverty in order to bring comfort to the realm of misery, of the afflicted, of the abandoned. What I write is no exaggeration, it is not based on flights of fancy, but is history, luminous history.

The reader, to form a clear idea of the admirable figure of Cardinal di Belmonte, great son of great Naples, whose biography I am writing, should glance at what Count Stanislao Pecci, great-nephew of Pope Leo XIII and Minister of the Sovereign Order of Malta to the Holy See, said of him. Here are his words: «In the not brief period in which I had frequent occasions of being in contact with him, one thing always appeared to me outstanding, namely the perfect and very rare balance between the most evident candor of his sentiments as a priest and the man of this world, who lives in this world and exercises his virtues.

And this showed itself in his every gesture and in every word of his, which never lacked good humor and gentlemanly wit.

A great gentleman, indeed, in the noblest sense of the word, his simplicity struck everyone who approached him, even for the first time and, awakening a most lively sympathy, immediately created the state of mind most favorable to a respectful yet confident disposition.

It does not seem to me even necessary to speak of the holy life he led, which, moreover, was mirrored in his constant and unchanging serenity, to which contributed an evident and intelligent good sense, which he made manifest in speaking of any subject whatever, or in discussing some question to which he always brought the liveliest and most youthful interest».

The whole life of the late Cardinal di Belmonte shines with simplicity, with goodness, with marvellous supernatural elevations; it is like that of Saint Pius X, of whom he was an intimate friend and great admirer.

Before beginning the life of Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, it is necessary to say something of the parents of this man of God, light and ornament of the Holy Roman Church. Of his genealogy I say little. Its history would fill many pages; I write only what is necessary for the purpose I have set myself.

Cardinal Granito has two surnames: the first is that of his own people; the second, that is, Pignatelli, he acquired by privilege, as we shall see further on.

The Granito family is a patrician family coming from the city of Salerno; the Pignatelli is one of the oldest of Naples.

The founder of the latter seems to descend from the Lombards. In 1102 one of them, Lucio, went to Naples, settled there, formed a family, and he and his descendants always enjoyed excellent esteem.

It is told that the king of Sicily, Roger II, went to war with Comnenus, emperor of the Greeks. One of his captains, Landolfo, assaulted the imperial palace in Constantinople, penetrated almost every part of it, even the kitchen, where, as proof of his daring, he took three silver pots and brought them to Naples to the Sovereign, who, as a testimony of gratitude, gave them back to the conqueror as a family emblem and as a surname.

The Pignatelli, naturally, over the centuries divided into several branches and gave to society and to the Church men who shone for spotless virtues and for depth of intellect.

Innocent XII — 1691†1770 — descends from the Pignatelli: he was a shrewd and scrupulous Pontiff. He put an end to nepotism; he often said: «My nephews are the poor».

In times closer to ours we have the beautiful figure of Giuseppe Pignatelli, a Jesuit, 1737†1812, who distinguished himself by exceptional piety. Pius XI, on 21 May 1933, raised him to the honors of the Holy Altars, proclaiming him Blessed, and in the year 1954 Pius XII numbered him among the Saints.

Angelo Granito, Marquis of Castellabate, of the seggi of Salerno, was the father of our Cardinal. Angelo was born in Naples on 20 October 1812 and from childhood showed himself lively, intelligent and very fond of study.

He soon learned, with singular profit, the Italian, Latin and French languages. He became familiar with the classics; he had a great passion for the Greek language and became one of the best Hellenists of his time.

He studied mathematics, history, philosophy, theology; he followed a course in civil and canon law; he loved music greatly, played the piano well, studied counterpoint, harmony and composition. Having a fine, harmonious bass voice, he sang at private gatherings for charity concerts, and very often in churches.

On 13 January 1833 he married Donna Carolina Carafa, of the Carafa della Stadera, second daughter of Don Francesco, Duke of Andria, and of the Duchess Donna Teresa Caracciolo di Santobuono. From this marriage he had twin daughters, who passed into eternity immediately after baptism. Afterwards he was father of another little daughter, who was given the name Maria Teresa Alfonsina.

On 30 September 1836 he lost his wife: the Marchioness Donna Carolina Carafa! Don Angelo, who loved her so much, wept, grieved, felt deep sadness in his soul, became sorrowful and pensive!

After some time had passed following this misfortune, he undertook journeys for study. He visited France, England, Austria. After about a year's absence from Naples he returned calmer and resumed his life of deep study.

Around 1838 his relatives advised him to take a second wife, because, having had no male child by the first, his noble house would die out. He accepted the advice. He met Donna Francesca Giuseppina Paola Pignatelli Aymerich, of Spanish origin, an heiress, princess of Belmonte, Marchioness of Galatone, Duchess of Acerenza, Countess of Copertino.

She was not only noble, but also beautiful and virtuous.

Don Angelo was captivated by the gifts of this angel of goodness, and in 1838, before the altar of God, he swore fidelity and love to her. Donna Francesca brought to the Granito people a vast store of titles. The Granito family, through this marriage, underwent a true transformation. It had belonged to the baronial families until the beginning of 1600; in that century, through the acquisition of the fief of Castellabate and through the merits of Parise III, it passed among the marquisal families and remained there until 1838, when, through the marriage of Don Angelo to J. Aymerich, it became a princely family, receiving other titles as well.

In the spring of 1844 the Marquis Don Angelo went to Rome with his mother, his wife and his two little daughters to visit His Holiness Gregory XVI, who received him gladly together with the family and remained with him conversing of history and archaeology for about an hour.

At the time when Pius IX, forced to flee from Rome because of the revolution of the day, resided in Naples as the guest of Ferdinand II, at the beginning of 1848 he went to visit the Great Archive and was received by Prince Don Angelo, who was its Superintendent, and where he also found the consort, Princess Paolina, who with singular respect kissed the hand of the persecuted Pontiff; he, with Francesca Paola Pignatelli Aymerich, remained for some time conversing with the Superintendent, and finally blessed him with his wife, and extended the blessing to all the family.

Don Angelo had vast learning; he wrote the History of the conspiracy of the prince of Macchia and of the occupation of the Austrian arms in the kingdom of Naples in 1707.

He also published a Greek grammar and various articles for interesting journals. His soul was dominated by upright and precise principles; he never boasted of his titles. He often used to say: Titles are zeros, which acquire value from the number of personal merits.

In 1861 he was struck by a grave illness, which he bore with truly Christian resignation. Seeing death near, he asked for the Sacraments and received them with deep devotion. Before expiring he said: I want no luxury of funeral, nor flowers; but prayers and holy Masses.

He fell asleep in the Lord in Naples, on 29 June 1861.

The mother of our Cardinal, Donna Francesca, was eminently Christian; she practized all the virtues and especially charity; a great part of her patrimony she distributed to the poor, in whom she saw the image of Jesus Christ.

She was very devout to Our Lady of Sorrows.

In her younger years, when cholera raged terribly in Naples, she feared this disease, and one day, throwing herself at the feet of Our Lady, she begged her not to let her die of so ugly an illness. And while she prayed she saw the picture of the Virgin surrounded by vivid light. She understood that that light was for her a sign of protection.

She was an enemy of the things of the world. Only in the teachings of the religion of Christ did she find supreme joy.

This exemplary woman gladdened the house with eight children: Chiara, Gioacchino, Gennaro, Maria della Mercede, Anna, Giulia, Livia and Laura.

In the house she was a true angel of goodness; she preached to her children first by example and then by word. Religious practices did not find her slack to the last moments of her life; she always throbbed with the purest love for the Lord.

She never relaxed her fasts; to those who tried to hinder her she answered: Fasting keeps health well and makes one live longer than usual.

She was the priestess of the house, where she lived as the strong woman of Sacred Scripture. She died on 30 August 1911, saintly, with an angelic smile on her lips.

From these parents, true Christians, of noble spirit and profound intelligence, Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte was born.

In the pleasant and evocative city of Naples Don Gennaro was born on 10 April 1851. He was baptized in the parish of San Marco di Palazzo by the Very Rev. Parish Priest Don Andrea Mancinelli; besides the name of the protector of Naples, at the pious wish of his relatives, other names were given to him.

From his tender years he loved Priests, the Church, prayer, works of piety. We do not know when and where he made his First Communion. At the age of nine he had the great misfortune of losing his beloved father; for so grave a misfortune he wept much, suffered much. For several days he appeared sorrowful and pensive. Sensitive, intelligent, devout souls suffer more than others at the loss of loved ones. Fr. Ludovico da Casoria, famous apostle of flowering Franciscan charity, founder of the Grey Friars, at the death of his mother — writes Cardinal Capecelatro — wept bitterly at her loss and for a certain time seemed quite other than he had been before. The beloved Arcangelo, for so Fr. Ludovico was called in the world; cheerful, festive, companionable with all, became sad, taciturn. He avoided companions and friends, often had eyes swollen with tears and even cut short the conversation of anyone who spoke to him of his Mother; for several days he refused his usual food, content with what scarcely sufficed to sustain him». Similar was the state of mind of D. Gennaro at the loss of the adored Father whom he loved so much.

Don Gennaro began his studies at home together with his brother Gioacchino and after some time took lessons with the Canons Regular of Piedigrotta.

In 1865, the Jesuits having set up a truly model college in the Villa Borghese at Frascati, called Mondragone, Don Gennaro applied to enter and his application was accepted. There he remained for four years, making excellent progress in the humanistic studies, winning the admiration of teachers and fellow students for his intelligence, for his sentiments of goodness and rectitude. He was one of the seven who earned the title of Founders of the college of Mondragone.

At the age of 18, in 1869, he sat the examination for the baccalaureate in philosophy in Rome, at the Roman College, and succeeded with excellent results. Afterwards he returned to Naples, where he applied himself to the study of the fine arts and especially of music and painting. He played the violin well and often painted pictures.

Don Gennaro made his entrance into Neapolitan society with the title of Count of Copertino and was well received there, not only for his social position, but also for his brilliant spirit, so rich in exquisite kindness.

It is told that in a drawing room a young man, thinking to throw him a quip, asked him whether he used the title of Count only in winter, to which Don Gennaro replied: «I use it in summer too, because at that time it is useful to me to protect myself from the chills of my friends». The reply was applauded.

Don Gennaro, in his Naples, delighted in hunting, gymnastics, fencing and dancing. He also thought of devoting himself to commercial life and for several months attended the Neapolitan Commercial Bank of Credit and Construction. During the period of his life at home he traveled as a tourist to learn, to enrich his culture still more. On one of his very long journeys, before returning to Naples he stopped a few days in Rome, where he asked to be received in audience by Pope Pius IX.

The Vicar of Christ was very generous to the young Count. He was then holding in the Consistory hall an assembly of Cardinals and arranged for the Count of Copertino to attend. With a heart throbbing with joy he took part.

How glad Don Gennaro was at such kindness of the Pontiff, how he rejoiced in the depth of his soul, and what emotion he felt finding himself in the presence of the Pope and of the Princes of the Holy Roman Church! He felt in his heart something new, a joy never felt before. Returned to Naples, he told his household and his friends with enthusiasm the great honor he had received in the Vatican.

Don Gennaro loved pleasant conversation and above all dressing elegantly; he seemed like Francis of Assisi when he was greeted as «Flower of the youth».

A Spanish publication of June 1929 gives the features of the Prince in his springtime years: «He shines, one would say with the poet, at first sight, a virgin flower of youth on his face». His figure is slender, his bearing finely gentlemanly, his eyes clear and intelligent, his gaze deep.

The Count of Copertino, for his nobility, for his ancestry, seemed destined in social life to great joys, to immense honors.

But the ways of Divine Providence are great, mysterious, unsearchable!

Behold, our Don Gennaro bids a farewell for ever to the world and its attractions: he consecrates himself to God.

Naples, at the time of Don Gennaro's youth, had as shepherd of souls a learned, humble, pious Archbishop, Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza, a man of holy life, an intimate friend of the Granito family. When he died, on 29 September 1877, Don Gennaro was present at his passing and kept loving vigil with a few other persons through the night around the body.

Silvestro Guzzolino Abbot, a native of Osimo, after he was ordained a priest, at the horrible sight of the corpse of an illustrious relative of his, said: «Ego sum quod hic fuit, quod hic est ego ero». At 50 he left Osimo, sought solitude, gave himself up to harsh penances, and became a glorious Saint of the Catholic Church. An almost similar episode is found in the life of Don Gennaro. Contemplating the corpse of Cardinal Riario Sforza, he meditated on death, thought of eternal destinies and conceived the idea of abandoning the world and embracing the ecclesiastical state. Before formally taking this decision, he prayed, he prayed much.

One day, incognito, in hunting dress, he went to the abbey of Cava dei Tirreni, where he revealed his ideals to the learned Benedictine, Abbot Don Guglielmo Sanfelice. What this most worthy son of Saint Benedict said to him we do not know; we know only that after this visit he appeared sad and taciturn. After careful reflection, he made known to his mother and to the family his wish to enter the ecclesiastical militia as a secular priest.

His mother was glad, his relatives were glad at his fine decision. On 12 March 1878 Don Gennaro put on the cassock in the House of the Virgins in Naples and on 15 June he received the tonsure. On that occasion he met and made friends with Don Benedetto Bonazzi, who later was Archbishop of Benevento, a man of great learning, author of a most valued Greek dictionary.

Don Gennaro was ordained Subdeacon on 21 December 1878. Deacon on 22 March 1879.

When Don Gennaro lived in his own lands, the Neapolitan clergy was rich in learned men: «Cardinal Gennaro Portanova, Cardinal Giuseppe Prisco, the canons: Sanseverino, Signoriello, Calvanesi, Mgr. Salvatore Talamo. These were the exponents of the fine Neapolitan philosophical family, who not only in the South, but throughout Italy prepared the mild climate of the Encyclical «Aeterni Patris», launched by Leo XIII at the dawn of his glorious pontificate, an encyclical which aroused a grand Thomistic movement in the

Catholic world». Beside these giants in the field of thought and piety Don Gennaro lived his youth, and they communicated to him a fascination of zeal and a deep love of study.

After the death of Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza, Leo XIII appointed Abbot Guglielmo Sanfelice Archbishop of Naples. The newly elected, on the eve of his triumphal entry into the see of the Diocese, chose as his traveling companion the cleric Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte. Two days after the entry, Cardinal Sanfelice went to the Palace of the Princess of Belmonte, mother of Don Gennaro, and said to her: «Princess, Gennarino, your son, I will take with me and he will remain with me; he will be my private secretary». «I am most happy, answered the pious woman; let him come, with God's help, with God's blessing». They set out.

One of the most beautiful works of the heart of Christ on earth was undoubtedly the creation of the Priest. Priests, according to the thought of Christ, are the light of the world, the salt of the earth. To Priests, in the person of the Apostles, Christ said: «Go into the world, as the Father has sent me, I send you; preach the gospel, baptize, forgive sins. Know that whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you, the insult falls upon me».

The Priest is Christ on earth, «Alter Christus».

And behold, our Don Gennaro receives the great priestly dignity, becomes, that is, the representative of the Redeemer of peoples.

On 7 June 1879, the octave of Pentecost, Cardinal Sanfelice in the Cathedral of Naples laid his hands upon his head and consecrated him Minister of the Sanctuary. How great was the joy of the new Levite cannot be described, cannot be imagined.

The day after the ordination, the feast of the Most Holy Trinity, the Rev. Don Gennaro celebrated in the parish church of Santa Maria degli Angeli; present were his relatives, a great part of the Neapolitan nobility, his friends; among them was his mother, who, in ecstasy, attended the holy Sacrifice of her son, shedding tears of joy.

The Count of Copertino was a Priest after God's own heart, he understood wonderfully the poetry of his ministry, and therefore carried out everywhere a luminous apostolate of good.

After the Ordination, Don Gennaro continued his sacred studies, still remaining in the Bishop's palace.

He took charge of the private administration of the Archbishop, of the diocesan Archive and of various works of a religious character. Appointed Canon, Don Gennaro was assiduous at the Choir; even when unwell he attended with edifying piety.

In 18811 he was appointed Ecclesiastical Superior of the Nursing Sisters, called Daughters of St. Anne, of whom he not only looked after the spiritual side, but also provided a House in Naples, on which he spent a good part of his patrimony.

Don Gennaro, in the first years of his priestly life, adorned the Church with the splendor of his piety and with growing zeal for all good works.

The Bishop, in the act of consecrating the Priest, infuses into his soul piety, zeal, a transcendent love. In the Catholic Church, mystical sheepfold of Christ, we find a veritable army of Priests rich in these gifts, who have shown flowering charity towards every misfortune, who have wept with the weeping of the unhappy, have struggled to comfort the sorrowful, and have seen in the abandoned, the ragged, the forsaken the sweet image of Christ.

If we examine the life of St. Charles Borromeo, of St. Vincent de Paul, of Cottolengo, of Cardinal Guglielmo Massaia, of Father Ludovico da Casoria, of the victim D. Gnocchi, of the present Supreme Pontiff and of so many others, we see at once that they sang marvellously in the kingdom of the wretched a canticle of supernatural love.

One of these is without doubt Cardinal Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte. His whole life speaks of charity, but luminous gleams of boundless love he showed with those struck by the earthquake of Casamicciola.

Ischia is an island of the Tyrrhenian Sea at the northern entrance of the Gulf of Naples, mountainous, very well known for its Volcano, Mount Epomeo, very active in antiquity and in the Middle Ages, dormant since 1301.

Casamicciola has smiling hills, where vineyards, pine woods and fragrant flowers abound; it has a mild climate, pure and perfumed air, celebrated thermal springs, and is rich in enchanting panoramas. Like a sentinel, before it on an islet stands the majestic castle of Alfonso I of Aragon, which speaks of the great and the powerful who once were. The whole island of Ischia, kissed by the sea, with the charm of its beauties and its smiles, offers visitors something sublime, mysterious, enchanting. In every age it was celebrated by poets, and it is frequented by tourists and bathers.

It has often known eruptions and earthquakes; the last was that of 28 July 1883, which brought desolation to its lands, but especially to Casamicciola, a municipality which then numbered little more than 400 inhabitants. It razed it to the ground; only three or four houses remained unharmed.

The fatal news reached Naples at night by telegraph. The citizens were shaken, perplexed, deeply grieved. Don Gennaro, as soon as he heard of it, felt immense pity for the victims struck by so great a misfortune and, without losing time, decided to leave for the scene of the disaster. He went very early, on the morning of 28 June, to the harbor, sought four sturdy sailors, spoke to them of the catastrophe that had struck Casamicciola, and begged them to take him in a boat of theirs to that place.

The sons of Naples have feeling, they have heart, they are generous! «Let us go», they answered him, and pointed out the boat to him. He climbed in, sat down, they got in too and drove it forcefully towards the shore of Casamicciola, where they landed.

Don Gennaro, when he set foot there, saw the desolation which the earth tremor had sown; he stood with wide-open eyes — the sailors related — and abundant tears bathed his face! When the emotion had somewhat passed, he went to the ruins of a house all too well known to his mind and to his heart; there he bloodied his hands to extract the body of Mgr. Mennella, Coadjutor Bishop of Ischia. In desolation he gave the poor victim a religious burial. Afterwards he was seen turning to right and to left, tireless, to dress the wounded, to succor the survivors, to pull the dead and the dying from the ruins. Amid so many human calamities Don Gennaro passed like the Angel of consolation!

A writer of the time affirms that this pious Priest at Casamicciola, in the terrible hours after the disaster — all who had the good fortune to approach him, all who heard from him the word of charity and of fatherly love, recognized in him the example of the rarest virtues. In the intensity of so great a disaster, he performed miracles of courage and industry, of tirelessness and physical strength to draw the buried from the rubble, risking his own life to save that of others. He passed by no misery without relieving it with the comfort of his gentle word and the effective support of his help.

On Friday, 30 July, the Archbishop of Naples Monsignor Sanfelice arrived at Casamicciola. He appeared like a vision of love and hope. The excellent Prelate had the heart of a most loving father for the hungry, for all the children of the immense misfortune. He felt in his soul those flames of charity which blazed in the heart of Christ. He gave immensely in alms in that kingdom of immense miseries.

In all his work of good he always had at his side the young and energetic Priest D. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte. These two intrepid athletes of ineffable charity, having fulfilled their merciful mission at Casamicciola, returned to Naples to help the wounded who had been brought there.

It is good to recall that Archbishop Sanfelice said to the Governor of the Pilgrims: «If in the Hospital you no longer have wards for the victims of the earthquake, use the Church as a ward; if linen is lacking, use the Altar cloths; if glasses are lacking, make use of the chalices».

Only the charity taught by Christ is capable of arousing in souls such self-denial, such compassion.

In the summer of 1884 Naples was visited by a terrible scourge: cholera. «The insidious disease passed like a cutting scythe through a field of ripe wheat». In every part of the city, sick, dying, victims. Many citizens, several nobles, as soon as they heard of the cholera, left their homes, fled far away, sought the mountains. D. Gennaro did not go away. He left his princely palace, threw himself into the midst of the danger, and there remained like an intrepid warrior on the field of sacrifice and sorrow. By night and by day he passed from one palace to another, from one hospital to another, from one hovel to another. The ardent zeal of his soul drove him into the midst of the sorrowing to share with them their hardships, their pains, their tears, to raise their crushed spirits to immortal hopes, to bring the souls of the dying to the immortal homeland, to the Kingdom of God.

Archbishop Sanfelice was moved before this sentinel of sorrow and, so that he might fulfill his ministry completely, gave him the faculty of administering the Sacrament of Confirmation.

In the life of Mother Gattorno, foundress of the daughters of St. Anne, in volume II, p. 73, written by Fr. Fiocchi S. J., we read that during the cholera of Naples «D. Gennaro di Belmonte went tirelessly through the hospitals, through the houses, administering the Sacraments, comforting with fatherly word and being generous in every way, encouraged others to give themselves generously to that merciful assistance». The expressions of the heart of our Cardinal, throughout his life, were boundless. He never cared for riches.

When he lived as Cardinal in Corso d’Italia, in Rome, cunning thieves one day entered his palace and laid hands precisely on the place where he kept rings, valuables, family keepsakes, decorations. They carried everything away. When he noticed, he did not grieve at all; to friends who expressed regret for the theft committed against him, he answered smiling: «We must not worry about the incident: what the thieves took was unused, now it is in circulation».

Justice wanted absolutely to seek out and arrest the authors of the theft, but he, recalling the words of the Redeemer: «Do good to those who do you harm», employed every means so that the inquiry into the culprits would die before being born.

D. Gennaro had properties in Spain, of immense value, and he donated them all to the Handmaid Sisters of the Sacred Heart.

The Capuchin Friars of the Church of Regina Pacis in Fiuggi needed an organ and had no means to buy it. They made their wish known to their Cardinal Protector, Don Gennaro, and he ordered that the organ be built at once.

A very dear friend of his, Canon Giovambattista Trovalusci, having pointed out to the Cardinal one day that he spent too much, he answered: Monsignor, it is necessary to lighten one's luggage to enter the Kingdom of God.

The life of Cardinal di Belmonte, especially in his last years, that is, when he withdrew from the palace of the Holy Office to Vatican City, to the building of Santa Marta, was very poor. Monsignor Francesco Rossi Stockalper, Liberian Canon, who lived with the Cardinal when he was Nuncio in Vienna, relates that Don Gennaro, needing handkerchiefs, asked him roughly the price and, finding it high, exclaimed: «They cost dearly, I am not in a position to spend such a sum; I shall try to make do with a sheet, and have handkerchiefs made from it».

When he died, his relatives told us, he had absolutely nothing in his room.

After the earthquake of which we spoke in the preceding chapter, Cardinal Sanfelice set out for Rome to inform Pope Leo XIII of the immense damage caused by the frightful earth tremor at Ischia, and especially at Casamicciola. He asked for an audience and it was granted at once.

He spoke to the Pope of the surviving population, without roof and without bread, in need of clothing, deprived of spiritual and moral guidance. He told the Holy Father that the Bishop of the Diocese lay in bed paralyzed, and that the Coadjutor had died under the rubble.

At this sorrowful story a feeling of profound sadness invaded the soul of the Vicar of Christ.

He sent to Ischia Monsignor Gennaro Portanova, a man of holy life, who was afterwards Archbishop of Reggio Calabria and later Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

In the audience which Cardinal Sanfelice had with Leo XIII he presented his traveling companion, D. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte. The Pontiff cast a glance at the face of the young Priest and discovered in his soul treasures of exceptional goodness. He appointed him, in April 1884, his Domestic Prelate. After this appointment they returned to Naples and Cardinal Sanfelice urged D. Gennaro to prepare for the doctorate in Sacred Theology. He obeyed. He prepared with exceptional care, and on 19 September 1884 he sat the examinations, brilliantly obtaining the doctorate.

D. Gennaro, in Naples, was a brother of the Confraternity of the Whites: Canon of the Chapter, he received the appointment of Co-visitor for the Diocese and that of Pro-secretary of the Holy Visitation. His name was widely known in the ecclesiastical field.

In 1886 the Holy Father Leo XIII called him to Rome and said to him: «I wish the Neapolitan Catholics to enter resolutely into administrative life». He entrusted to him the task of preparing and guiding them in the elections that were near.

With humility D. Gennaro accepted the charge and promised the Pontiff that he would not only obey but would put to work all his energies for the success of the undertaking.

According to the spirit of the «Non expedit», of a Decree of the Sacred Penitentiary of 10 October 1874 and of a Brief of Pius IX of 1877 to the Council of Catholic Youth, the Catholic democratic forces were not to take part at the polls in Italy… «Neither electors, nor elected».

But Leo XIII saw the necessity of taking part, to prevent men incapable of serving the good of the State from coming to power, and in part abolished the contrary laws. Pius X modified them, inviting Catholics to unite in order to come to power.

Benedict XV, in 1919, abolished them definitively, and Catholics entered fully into Italian political life, first in the Italian Popular Party and later in Christian Democracy.

In 1945 the vigilant Magisterium of the Church issued directives on the electoral duty, in which absenteeism from elections is censured.

In our times, according to the teaching of the Church, all those who have the right to vote, of whatever condition, sex and age, without any exception, are in conscience strictly obliged to make use of this right.

Catholics, say the provisions on the matter, must give their vote to those Candidates or lists of Candidates who respect and defend the observance of the divine law, the rights of Religion and of the Church.

Our D. Gennaro may be said to have been the first, after the «Non expedit»…, to fight in the administrative elections.

After the pontifical Audience, he returned to his homeland, approached relatives and persons he knew, and spoke to all of the delicate charge he had received from the Holy Father, and he did so much and said so much that, despite the obstacles set by the Freemasons, the anticlericals and all the enemies of the Church, in the elections of that year the Catholics won a marvellous victory: with flags flying they entered the Municipality of Naples.

Everyone knew that the organization of so memorable a success was to be ascribed to Mgr. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte.

After the brilliant result of the municipal elections, D. Gennaro, to defend the rights of the Church, to keep Catholics united and urge them to fight the battles of true national good, bought the newspaper «LA LIBERTÀ», of which he was Publisher and shrewd Editor. He enlarged its format, enriched its news service, gathered around himself collaborators of high intelligence.

He kept the paper for two years, and this was the «golden period of La Libertà».

Much money he spent on the good press; he almost exhausted what remained of his paternal patrimony.

He never cared about money; he considered it simply as a means necessary for living; he had great trust in the Providence of God; he meditated assiduously on the great words of Christ: «Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven».

As a simple Priest, as Bishop, as Cardinal, D. Gennaro aroused sympathy in every class of people, as we shall see, because he personified goodness.

Delicate and honorary assignments were entrusted to him everywhere.

He was greatly loved and esteemed in the Sovereign Order of Malta. On 7 November 1931 he received there the appointment of Bailiff Grand Cross of Honor and Devotion, with assignment to the Grand Priory of Naples and Sicily; and then, upon designation by Pope Pius XI, that of Bailiff Grand Cross of Justice and of Grand Prior of Rome, according to Council Decree dated 18 December 1937 No. 2794.

A man, whatever class he belongs to, if he wishes to enjoy trust, if he wishes to win respect in social life, must walk under the watchful gaze of God, who sees all and is not seen. He must have uprightness as his companion before God; he must keep high the sentiment of faith and of morality.

All those who live with these ideals, with these maxims, with these wisest principles, find sympathy everywhere, honorary posts, and pass blessed among the people. And Cardinal di Belmonte throughout his life lived in the atmosphere of the truths I have set out here; therefore assignments of great importance were entrusted to him.

The Holy See has diplomatic relations with many governments, Catholic and non-Catholic, and sends to them, on great occasions, at great feasts and also in hours of great mourning, its representatives, who speak in the name of the Pontiff.

Monsignor Gennaro Granito di Belmonte held important assignments in various nations which had bonds of friendship with the Holy See.

At the beginning of 1893, with the consent of the Archbishop, he left Naples and went to Rome. He lived in the house of his brother D. Gioacchino.

The Holy Father wanted him in the Secretariat of State, at the Congregation of Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs, without stipend, allowing him to keep the prebend of his canonry at Naples.

In June of the same year he was sent as Ablegate to bring the cardinal's biretta to Monsignor Lecot, Archbishop of Bordeaux.

On that occasion President of the Republic Carnot named him Officer of the Legion of Honor.

On 24 April 1896 the Holy Father Leo XIII sent a special mission to Russia for the coronation of Tsar Nicholas II and Mgr. D. Gennaro Granito was part of it as Counsellor. On that occasion he was decorated with the Commandery of St. Anne of Russia.

In April 1897 he was appointed Counsellor of the Apostolic Nunciature in Paris, where he went on 3 May 1897.

In the same year he was chosen as Counsellor of the Extraordinary Mission which H. H. Leo XIII sent to London to take part in the jubilee festivities for the 60th year of reign celebrated by Her Majesty

Queen Victoria. — In 1899, after the death of the President of the Republic Félix Faure, Mgr. Granito, in his capacity as Counsellor of the Nunciature, was able to go to the Congress of Versailles to witness the election of Mr. Loubet to the Presidency of the Republic. Shortly afterwards, in the month of March, Monsignor Clari, Apostolic Nuncio, died in Paris and Mgr. Granito headed that Nunciature as Chargé d'Affaires for four months. When the new Nuncio was appointed, Mgr. Granito, decorated with the Commandery of the Legion of Honor, returned to Italy.

In 1911 we find him again in London, as Head of a Pontifical Mission, to bring there to King George V the congratulations of His Holiness on the occasion of the coronation. In this mission the young Monsignor Eugenio Pacelli, the present Pontiff, took part as prelate.

In all these journeys Mgr. Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte was greatly appreciated for his goodness, for his gentlemanly bearing, for his innate courtesies.

He had the greatest regard for his missions, thinking himself the representative not of a kingdom of this world, but of the Kingdom of Christ, of the Catholic Church.

Of the honors and praises he received everywhere Mgr. di Belmonte was never proud; great was his humility; perhaps in moments of honor he exclaimed from the depths of his soul: «Laus Deo».

In the Vatican milieu Mgr. di Belmonte was well known and highly esteemed for his good and exceptional virtues. But the one who knew and esteemed him most was the great Latinist, the learned Pontiff Leo XIII, who, to give him clear testimony of his august esteem, in November 1899 appointed him titular Archbishop of Edessa and Apostolic Nuncio to Belgium. As soon as Don Gennaro learned of this appointment he bowed his head to the wishes of the Pontiff, which for him were the wishes of God. He prepared for the Episcopal consecration with prayers, with penances, and finally with a course of spiritual exercises which he made among the sons of St. Alphonsus M. de Liguori in Via Merulana in Rome.

On 26 November 1899 he was consecrated Bishop in the Church of the Daughters of St. Anne in Rome, in Via Merulana, by His Eminence Cardinal Mariano Rampolla del Tindaro, Secretary of State. The co-consecrating Bishops were Mgr. Carlo Caputi and Mgr. Casimiro Gennari, who was later Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. During the Consecration Don Gennaro had eyes veiled with tears. How much those tears said!

His mission as Apostolic Nuncio begins. The Church, as we said in the preceding chapter, has diplomatic relations with very many nations. In choosing her representatives abroad she takes particular care.

For their formation she has established in Rome the Academy of Noble Ecclesiastics, where Priests are received for their diplomatic training. These must have these principal marks: deep attachment to the Holy Roman Church, excellent morals, good intelligence, a soul rich in goodness and courtesy, freedom from physical defects.

Vatican diplomacy, among its Apostolic Nuncios, boasts classic figures and one of them is that of Monsignor di Belmonte.

At the end of December he left for Brussels, his destination; he presented his Credentials in time to take part there in the customary official festivities of New Year's Day 1900. During the time he was Nuncio in Belgium Queen Victoria of England died and he was charged with presenting, on behalf of His Holiness Leo XIII, condolences to the new King Edward VII.

In 1903, while he was returning to Italy with regular leave, the Holy Father Leo XIII fell gravely ill. Mgr. di Belmonte left Naples, hurried to Rome, lovingly visited the illustrious sick man and then stayed to recite prayers with other prelates in the Pontiff's private Chapel. Leo XIII died on 22 July 1903 and was succeeded by Pius X. After the death of the said Pontiff, Don Gennaro paid his respects to Cardinal Oreglia di S. Stefano, Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church, and set out again for Brussels. In Belgium Mgr. di Belmonte left lasting traces. He defended Christian principles before all, preached virtue by example and by word, was protector and comforter of so many Italians scattered in those lands.

The King with all his family, the Court, the Dukes, the nobles of the Kingdom, the popular masses had for him deep sentiments of affection and veneration. Days of great activity Cardinal di Belmonte passed in Brussels, but serene and tranquil.

In January 1904 the new Pontiff Pius X appointed Mgr. Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte Apostolic Nuncio in Vienna. He left Brussels in March of the same year, having to await his successor for the handing over of the Nunciature. On leaving, he was decorated by His Majesty King Leopold II with the great Cordon of St. Leopold of Belgium. His affairs having been settled, towards the end of March 1904 he went to Vienna and presented his Credentials to Emperor Francis Joseph. In June 1904 his jubilee for the 25th year of Priesthood fell due, but being abroad, he thought it fitting not to celebrate it publicly, but only spiritually.

In Austria Don Gennaro did not find the social horizon serene. Infiltrations of modernist principles had penetrated various circles and even among Catholics, and he watched and fought against modernism. In those times Josephinism was not entirely extinguished in Austria; the powerful demanded submission to their wishes from ecclesiastical persons; but Mgr. di Belmonte always firmly upheld the evangelical principle: «What is Caesar's is Caesar's, what is God's is God's».

In March 1908, in defense of the rights of the Church, he offended the sensibilities of certain political parties, with some ministers of the government in solidarity; all strove to remove the Apostolic Nuncio from Vienna. Vain were their efforts; the diplomatic Nuncio, a man of wide views, upright, sincere, an enemy of subterfuge and lies, remained at his post.

One day a Prelate who was Consultor of the Austro-Hungarian Embassy in Rome presented himself to Pius X. The Pontiff received with his usual kindliness the Prelate, who presented himself in the name of the Ambassador, but when he understood that the purpose of that visit was the recall of the Apostolic Nuncio from Vienna, he at once cut him short and, rising to his feet, in a proud and resolute tone of voice exclaimed: I have said no, and let it be no!

That Monsignor left the audience pale; he had understood that the time of Josephinist pique had passed.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the time, Count d'Aehrental, more than anyone sought to have the Nuncio removed from Vienna, because the latter in a letter had censured a lecture by a university professor not in conformity with the Orthodoxy of the Church. (See P. G. Dal Gal – S. PIO X PAPA – pp. 526-27).

Another reason why he sought to remove him was that the Nuncio strongly complained of the indiscretion of a newspaper, which published an item on a very delicate subject, which was to remain secret.

The contrasts of Cardinal di Belmonte with Minister d'Aehrental ought to be more fully illuminated in these pages; a complete narration of the facts would be needed, but the nearness of the times does not permit it. Certain it is that he acted as a great diplomat, as a faithful representative of the Church. The Rev. Monsignor Luigi Hudal, who knew Cardinal di Belmonte closely, wrote of him: «As Nuncio in Vienna his office was extraordinarily heavy, which did not prevent him from always preserving the dignity of count together with that of Prince of the Roman Church».

The Holy Father kept Mgr. Granito at his post for about three more years. He was Nuncio in Vienna for over a decade. The Supreme Pontiff had decided to hold a Consistory in 1910 and to have him return in the customary form, that is, as Cardinal.

The political events of Portugal did not allow the Holy Father to hold the Consistory as he had established. Mgr. Granito begged the Pontiff to accept his resignation as Nuncio, to ease the conduct of affairs in Austria, whose Minister of Foreign Affairs had let him know that for about three years he had no longer dealt with him. At this Pius X was extremely pleased, and showed him all his gratitude. At last Mgr. Granito left Austria. Before leaving Vienna, in 1910, His Majesty the Emperor honored him with the highest decoration usually given to foreigners, that is, the Grand Cross of St. Stephen of Hungary.

In the times when Mgr. Granito was Nuncio at the Court of Austria-Hungary, he received from the Holy Father the charge of crowning in his name the statue of the centuries-old, miraculous Virgin Mary, called «of Mariazell», venerated in the most distinguished Austrian Sanctuary.

In Austria he gave the episcopal Consecration to Mgr. Disger Colbry, Bishop of Kassa; to Mgr. Hittmair, Bishop of Linz, and to Mgr. Grovik, Abbot General of the oriental Religious called Mechitarists.

In June 1911 His Holiness Pius X wished to give a new proof of special benevolence to Mgr. Granito di Belmonte, as appears from the preceding chapter, appointing him his Special Envoy to represent him at the festivities of the Coronation of Their Majesties King George V and Queen Mary of England.

On returning from that mission, Monsignor, awaiting the Consistory, stayed in Naples with his mother, whose health was declining day by day. Towards the end of July, the weakness began to increase in the noble lady in a disquieting way; a strong aversion to food was added, her strength diminished; for the last ten days of the month she could no longer leave her bed. On 30 August 1911, without any special illness, she gently fell asleep in the Lord, surrounded by all her children. Don Gennaro, besides the care shared with his relatives, wished to comfort her with the last Sacraments and to give her all religious assistance to the last moments of life. Bitter anguish he felt in his soul at the loss of his adored mother.

Cardinals, after the Pope, are the highest dignities of the Catholic Church.

They form the Senate of the Vicar of Christ, are his co-workers and sometimes his representatives.

They are elected by the Pope and elect the Pope.

Originally the Cardinal was the titular Priest of a principal Church (Cardinal) of Rome. Until the fifteenth century the Cardinals did not exceed thirty, but in 1586 Pope Sixtus V fixed their number at seventy. The Sacred College, however, is rarely complete, because often some Cardinals die from one Consistory to the next. All Cardinals, even if simple priests, give their vote in the Councils; they have precedence over Patriarchs, Archbishops and Bishops, they are citizens of the Vatican, even if they live far away. Cardinals are divided into three orders: six of the suburbicarian Bishops, fifty of the Priests, fourteen of the Deacons.

The highest Cardinalatial dignities are: the Secretary of State, who is like the foreign minister of the Pontiff; the Cardinal Camerlengo, who looks after the goods of the Holy See; the Cardinal Vicar, who represents the Pope in Rome, in this historic city.

And among the Cardinals there is the Dean, who is first among equals and is Bishop of Ostia. Cardinals are freely created by the Roman Pontiff, chosen from among Bishops and Priests who have most distinguished themselves in the various branches of ecclesiastical activity. Monsignor Don Gennaro had so distinguished himself for the good of the Church, he had never said enough in the work of the apostolate; the fire of divine love never died out in his soul, the spread of the Kingdom of God was at the top of his thoughts, he always thought of sending souls to Paradise; the cry of his heart was: «Da mihi animas coetera tolle»; that is why he had the honor of the purple.

The circumstances having changed because of which the Pontiff had thought it fitting not to hold a Consistory for several years, moved by the vacancies that continually occurred in the Sacred College, towards the end of the year 1911 he announced that he would hold a Consistory for the good of the Church. He held it on 27 November 1911, and in it the Archbishop of Edessa, Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, was raised to the honors of the purple and was assigned the presbyteral title of Santa Maria degli Angeli. He resigned it three years later, on the death of Cardinal Agliardi, by option for the suburbicarian see of Albano.

With the death, in 1930, of Cardinal Vincenzo Vannutelli, Cardinal Granito di Belmonte succeeded him as Dean of the Sacred College in the Suburbicarian See of Ostia, attached to that office, and also in the office of Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Ceremonial.

Don Gennaro, as Cardinal, on three solemn occasions was Pontifical Legate: at the International Eucharistic Congress of Lourdes in July 1914, at the festivity of Orléans in 1921 for the Canonization of Joan of Arc, and at the Italian National Eucharistic Congress of Palermo in 1924.

Above all, wrote «L’OSSERVATORE ROMANO», notable was his work in the Congregation of Rites, also as Ponens of numerous Causes of Servants of God.

The Lord willed to gladden his life with a double joy: letting him attend the Beatification of his heroic diocesan Maria Goretti, to whom he was very devoted. Don Gennaro's great-nephew, Raimondo del Balzo, Duke of Presenzano, Counsellor at the Court of Appeal of Rome, confided to me that his uncle had told him one day, with the sentiments of the deepest humility, that Maria Goretti had appeared to him.

Cardinal di Belmonte worked much for the introduction of the cause of Beatification of his first Spiritual Master, the great Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza. For the Jubilee of the Redemption — 1933-1934 — he was Delegate of Pope Pius XI to open and to close the Holy Door of the Patriarchal Basilica of Saint Paul.

He took part in three Conclaves and entered that of 1939 as Dean of the Sacred College during the Vacant See on the death of Pius XI. He exercised that office exemplarily, with authority.

«There was no arduous and solemn circumstance in which he did not reveal his attachment to the Church and to the Vicar of Christ. It will suffice, among other things, as an indelible memory, the address of warm fidelity which he, also in the name of the Most Eminent Colleagues, addressed in December 1946 to the Holy Father. His words aimed to synthesize and echo the fervent addresses of homage and good wishes which on Christmas Eve he used to read at the Apostolic Throne and into which he poured the surges and assurances of his noble heart.»

The reader will find the address of 1946 further on.

Saint Charles Borromeo uttered one day this phrase: «It is not the purple that honors the Cardinal, but it is the Cardinal who must honor the purple».

Borromeo's expression Cardinal di Belmonte felt, made his own, practized; he accepted the purple in order to honor it; as soon as he received the appointment as Prince of the Church he humbled himself before God and promised Him to know Him more, to serve Him more faithfully until death. After these promises he was the Priest more than ever a lover of duty and of virtues.

Assiduous in his office at the Congregation of Ceremonial and of Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs, always ready in the others of which he was a member. Extraordinary joy he felt in the depths of his soul in assisting the Supreme Pontiff at the great functions in St. Peter's. In the dioceses of Albano and Ostia, his suburbicarian sees, he was most zealous, and poured out there almost all his financial resources.

At the solemn celebrations of the Parishes of Rome and outside Rome, in the Churches of Religious men and women, at Congresses, at Catholic assemblies, at sacred retreats, with his imposing person, his clear gaze, his gentle manner, he knew how to give a solemn tone of magnificence and splendor.

The words which Cardinal Merry del Val had written on a page of a small notebook in which he used to note the austere aspirations of his soul: «To find God in the sanctifying prose of daily duty. Silence and recollection. Prayer and activity. Sacrifice and love», although Don Gennaro did not know them, were the program of his very long life.

The Cardinal Protector is that Prince of the Holy Roman Church who, at the request of a religious society, is designated by the Supreme Pontiff as aid, counsellor and assistant to it.

Its origin goes back to the Middle Ages and properly to St. Francis of Assisi; in fact the holy Poor Man of God, between 1220-221, asked for and obtained from Pope Honorius III Cardinal Ugolino as Protector of his Order. The Seraphic saw the usefulness and the necessity of the Cardinal Protector and therefore prescribed in the rule that «the Friars should ask of the Holy Roman Church a Cardinal who should be gubernator, protector et corrector of the whole minorite brotherhood».

From St. Francis the Protectorate of Cardinals extended to other religious Orders, and little by little all felt the need of it.

The purpose of ecclesiastical Bodies in having a Cardinal Protector is to find in him the Patron, the wise counsellor, the one who must make known to the Holy See their needs and necessities. And Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte was protector of religious Orders of men and of women, of institutes, of various congregations in Italy and abroad. The religious bodies that had him as Protector were 44.

He, with this title, exercised in Religious Houses a wonderful apostolate. In the sacred enclosures where he set foot he appeared as the Angel of goodness, welcomed souls with fatherly clemency: to all he gave wise counsel, to all he dispensed smiles and blessings.

I have approached religious men and women and asked for news of him, as Protector, and in chorus they have answered me that «he was a beautiful soul, rich in piety, in luminous priestly sentiments, vibrant in all his manifestations with deep love of God».

The Very Rev. Fr. Benigno da S. Ilario, a Milanese, Minister General of the Capuchins, has written: «Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte was for thirty-three years Protector of our Order. Many times at General Chapters we approached him and listened to his wise words. We can affirm that in all his expressions, in all his judgments, in all his wishes there dominated a sentiment of exceptional goodness and a great interest for the good, for the progress of our Order.

In confirmation of what we attest, we are pleased to recall the speech he addressed on 5 May 1940 to our Predecessor, Very Rev. Father Donato da Welle, replying to the congratulations on the happy occasion of the XXV anniversary of the Protectorate.

«Most Reverend Father,

the dear Capuchin Friars have wished to underline in so kind and charitable a way the present occasion of the XXV year of my Protectorate towards their deserving Order.

I do not see it possible or right on my part to let everything pass in absolute silence. Your Very Rev. Paternity, with your affectionate invitation of the occasion, has made rain down upon my poor soul a precious, heavenly manna, made up of the spiritual treasure of thousands of Holy Masses and Communions offered generously for me to the Lord by the entire Capuchin family. The same Your Very Rev. Paternity, however, must allow me to express here publicly my heartfelt gratitude and to convey, through you, my thanks to all your sons in St. Francis.

Nor can I keep silent my admiration, my pleasure at the magnificent picture, on which master hands have fixed, in the most interesting details, the jubilee event, and which Your Very Rev. Paternity, accompanied by your General Definitory, was kind enough to present to me personally as a gift, on the very day of the anniversary.

As I had the pleasure of telling you at that meeting, I gladly repeat here that among the not few jubilees which my advanced age is making me see, this one of ours is one of those which most honors us, having represented, for so exceptional a period, among you the Supreme Pontiff, in accordance with the other intentions and devout dispositions of your Seraphic Founder, who was the first to implore and obtain from the Vicar of Jesus Christ the Cardinal Protector.

To make this my Jubilee of Protectorate yet more festive and pleasant there is added the happy coincidence of the Priestly Jubilees of Your Most Reverend Paternity, as well as of the Very Rev. Father Procurator General of the Order.

I am pleased to point it out because all together we are to raise the hymn of our moved thanksgiving to the Giver of every good, and spur ourselves on to ever greater virtue and holiness.

In pledge and confirmation of my lively, affectionate gratitude, may there descend upon you, Very Rev. Minister General, and upon each of your dear Capuchins my blessing, propitiator of «peace and good».

For Us the late Cardinal Dean was a soul rich in exceptional virtues, a true man of God, luster and ornament of the Sacred Purple, an eminent Protector of our Order».

The Superior General of the Daughters of St. Anne, Sister Sebastiana Pifferi, in a letter stated: «Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte was Protector of our Institute. All the Sisters who knew him affirm that he was gentle, serene, upright. Paternally he smiled and paternally he admonished, and often in his Neapolitan dialect. When he appeared in our House in Via Merulana, it was a feast for all the Religious. We shall never forget him, because for our Institute he was a Protector all zeal, a loving Father, the Angel of Comfort, every time misery knocked at our Houses».

The Very Rev. Father Filippo M. Ferrini, O. S. M., Confessor of the Pontifical Family and Postulator General of the Servants of Mary, writes thus: «I had occasion to know and to see often Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, Protector of our Order and living member of it, because he belonged to it as a fervent Tertiary. I remember him on the occasion of the VII Centenary of our Order, 2 February 1935, active, an excellent counsellor, and when in the Church of St. Marcellus in Rome he imparted Eucharistic Benediction to an immense crowd of people. Above all I remember his docility, his prudence, his far-sightedness, every time I asked him for counsel. I remember him assiduous at the functions of the S. C. of Rites, when Causes concerning our Religious were being treated.

The merits of Cardinal di Belmonte, as Protector of our Order, are many, and in it his Name will never be forgotten».

The relatives of Cardinal di Belmonte tell that when he lived at Montemario and at Santa Maria in the Vatican, very many religious men and women came to his residence, asking to speak with him, and he welcomed them with the greatest cordiality. Why did they go to him? The life of Convents, of Monasteries is beautiful, is mystical, is poetic, especially when embraced with true vocation and a spirit of sacrifice; it is the antechamber of Paradise. But unfortunately even in the sacred Cloisters crosses, tribulations, afflictions of spirit are not lacking. There is humanity and therefore frailty. And oh! how religious men and women, amid the miseries of life, seek a pious soul, a learned soul, to be enlightened, guided towards the arduous heights of Christian perfection. A very great part of the said souls who went to the Cardinal's residence in some way, indirectly, depended on him, he was their Cardinal Protector; but above all they sought him because he had a charm of goodness indescribable, because he spoke words of eternal life; they sought him for that something spiritual which emanated from his person. They found the protector, the comforter, the Priest who opened their hearts to immortal hopes.

A pious religious wrote: «Conversing with Cardinal di Belmonte, you seem to find yourself not before a man, but before a being who is free of all that savors of human miseries; in him two gazes always meet: that of the pupils, placid and serene, and that of the soul, blazing with supernatural light».

Don Gennaro held the office of Cardinal Protector with wisdom, with prudence, with a spirit of strict humility and deep self-denial; with this office he knew how to exercise in the Church of Christ, I repeat, a stupendous apostolate.

Cardinal di Belmonte succeeded Cardinal Agliardi as Bishop of Albano. As soon as he set foot in the Diocese, he studied every means to benefit souls and to bring them closer to God.

Arduous was his apostolate, because it unfolded between two wars in particularly difficult times.

He saw that in various places of the Diocese Churches were lacking, and with marvellous activity in a short time he caused them to rise. To his zeal, to his generosity is owed the parish of S. Maria delle Grazie at Marino, that of the Sacred Heart at Ciampino and at Nettuno, that of St. Philip at Cecchina with the respective Vicariates of Campoleone and of Pavona.

His fatherly heart felt very great joy when he saw rise, through the work of the Government, the Churches of Aprilia, of Pomezia, of Montello with the Vicariate of Bainsizza.

He saw in the Churches, the great Cardinal, the bulwarks of the faith of Christ, the sanctuaries of so many prayers and so many vows, the places most suited for the triumph of moral and social good; therefore his soul ardently desired that they should multiply.

Don Gennaro founded, in Albano and at Castel Gandolfo, the Pious Institute of the Catechist Sisters of the Immaculate and of St. Francis. He spent in his Diocese very much money on pious works. To make God known, to relieve miseries, to comfort the needy were the deepest, most heartfelt beatings of his heart.

He thought of even the smallest expenses of his Clerics of Liceo and Theology: he gave them books, clothes, medicines, the Breviary, when they were promoted to the Subdiaconate.

He possessed a sense of goodness, of compassion for all and especially for his Priests. When in the latter he found faults, he admonished them fatherly, corrected them; but when he found them obstinate in evil, he was inexorable, he punished severely.

In the Diocese of Albano he is remembered as an exemplary, charitable Shepherd, an incomparable Apostle of good. The Vicar General of Albano, Mgr. Giovanni B. Trovalusci, has recently written that Monsignor di Belmonte stripped himself of almost all he owned to help the Diocese of Albano.

No less interesting was Don Gennaro's zeal for the Diocese of Ostia. From 1931 to 1941 the Parish of Regina Pacis at Ostia was ruled by the Pallottine Don Giuseppe Ranocchini, an intelligent, most active priest, today Postulator General of the Order. He has described with a master's pen the varied activity which His Eminence Cardinal Granito carried out in that Diocese. He relates that the Cardinal ardently desired the teaching of Religion in the Schools, from Elementary to Liceo, spiritual assistance to the troops, to the Sisters, to the sick. He proposed various initiatives to educate the youth, such as theater, cinema, libraries, catechetical prize-givings. He rejoiced when these works were crowned with success, and grieved when they met obstacles from the wicked of the world.

The licentious life that went on on the beach of Ostia worried him greatly. The scandals of this place tormented his soul, palpitating with goodness and Faith. Every year he addressed to the Parish Priest a letter to be read and explained to the people in Church. In it he always set in view the great moral danger of the youth who went to the sea at Ostia. He recommended to the Priests and to the good faithful fervent prayers, so that spiritual ruin of souls might be avoided.

He had Catholic Action so much at heart, he made known its importance, its excellence, and never tired of recommending it to the Parish Priest. How he grieved and suffered when in June 1931, by order of the Head of Government, Benito Mussolini, all the Catholic clubs had to be closed and the keys of the premises handed over with the registers to the Militia! In that painful circumstance the Cardinal recommended to the Parish Priest and to the faithful prudence and prayer.

Catechetical instruction stood at the top of his thoughts; he wanted to know the number of pupils attending it, asked for a detailed report on such teaching in the government schools, and every year sent a representative of his to the prize-giving, which was always held with the greatest solemnity. Although the Parish Priest of the Lido of Ostia was a Religious, he treated him as a diocesan Priest. He showed himself grateful towards the Pallottines for having settled various financial pendencies with the contractors, left unpaid at the death of Cardinal Vannutelli.

Don Gennaro took great interest in the procedures to obtain the parochial Congrua; at his own expense he completed the finishing works of the Church; he watched over even the smallest things so that the Parish might progress in good from day to day.

The characteristic side of his care for the Parish was correspondence. For all problems concerning administration, the Religious Institutes, the Associations, conflicts with local Authorities, the Parish Priest always turned to the Cardinal, and found him ready to reply with exhaustive letters, all written in his own hand. The counsels he gave were precise; he saw clearly the knot of questions and with certainty expressed his thought.

Parish Priest Ranocchini writes that during the years of his priestly ministry at Ostia he received from the Cardinal about two hundred letters. A pity that all were lost when, on 20 September 1943, the order came to evacuate the Parish within 24 hours.

The rumor had spread that the evacuation would last a short time, whereas it was long, and all the houses, not excluding the Churches, were barbarously looted. The Cardinal's letters disappeared.

A great part of the refugees from Ostia then dispersed through Rome. Some found hospitality with relatives and friends. In this circumstance the Cardinal's charity shone marvellously. The provisions which he drew from the Vatican he sent to the Sisters, to the Infant Asylums, to the poor, keeping for himself only a few little things.

There were days when he distributed everything, not caring to suffer hunger. Pope Pius XII knew the sentiments of flowering charity of Cardinal Granito. The Very Rev. Father Ranocchini relates that in 1941 the Diocese of Ostia asked for a private audience with the Holy Father. It was granted. More than two thousand persons took part, among them the Parish Priest. The Cardinal was absent. The audience was very long: from 9.30 to 13.00. The Pontiff showed himself most kind to all. He took an interest in individual persons and in the various things of the Diocese. One of them said: «Our Cardinal takes great care of our Diocese». The Pontiff then smiled with pleasure, like a loving Father, and added: «I know that Cardinal Belmonte takes so much interest in the Diocese, that he loves his diocesans so much, that he lives for them. Be fond of him! I am so fond of him: he is for me like a papa». As he spoke these words the Pontiff had eyes veiled with emotion. All then understood how much affection bound these two magnanimous hearts.

Wishing to give an exact, precise, clear definition of Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, one that indicates the marvellous beatings of his heart, the surges of flowering goodness of his beautiful soul, one must salute him: Homo Dei.

He consecrated his long existence completely to the service of God and to the good of souls.
