To write of his spiritual, interior life is difficult, as it is difficult to write of all those who have practized the virtues to a heroic degree and have entered the luminous field of holiness.

The most solemn acts of the Servants of God, that is, the working of grace in their spirit, their intimate union with the Most High, the ineffable joy they experienced in prayer, in the contemplation of eternal destinies and their raptures in the regions of eternity will never be described.

St. Francis of Assisi, before being kissed by sister death, withdrew to Mount Alverna, to prepare there for the passage from time to eternity. History tells us that he received the Holy Stigmata, but who can narrate his sighs, his groans, the love that consumed him before receiving them and after having received them? Nobody, certainly.

And so we know nothing of the interior life of Cardinal di Belmonte, because he was humble, reserved, and never did a word escape his lips that hinted at his virtues and his nobility; and yet from his actions, which are pale reflections of his soul full of light, we can very well infer that he was a man wholly of God.

He loved the Lord immensely; He was his center, his sigh, the joy of his soul. He saw Him, read Him in created things, and from them he rose to the heavenly ones, to His kingdom of incomparable love.

Amid the many occupations of life, he thought also of the care of canaries, he loved them, he saw in them the greatness, the wisdom of God.

Prayer, meditation, holy reading, spiritual retreats were the dominant passions of his heart; until the last days of his life he recited the Breviary with singular devotion. He seemed to repeat with St. Augustine: «Psalterium meum, gaudium meum». Often, with surges of faith, he murmured ejaculatory prayers, raising himself to the Lord, his center, his treasure, his happiness. Every week, punctually, he approached the Sacrament of Penance, always seeking learned and virtuous confessors. The last, in order, was Father Ottavio Marchetti S. J.

The Most Eminent Cardinal understood that one cannot love God without loving one's neighbor and therefore extended the affection of his heart to all men, especially to the poor, in whom he saw the image of blessed Christ. He brought comfort to the kingdom of the afflicted, the forsaken, the abandoned: he died poor in order to relieve the poor. Such and so great was the love he felt for holy poverty that even after death he wished to have her as companion, as we shall see further on.

Don Gennaro was a Eucharistic soul. When he had to go away from home, before going out he visited with exceptional care Jesus the Host in his Chapel; he did the same on returning. When he arrived at Parishes, Convents, Monasteries, for reasons of office, before anything else he sought the Altar, the Tabernacle. In doubts, in adversities, in sorrows, in all the struggles of life he asked light and comfort of the Sovereign, of the hidden God. To the pious souls who approached him he advised frequent Communion, spiritual Communion, visits to Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament.

«These are the sources — he said — from which one must draw strength to walk unimpeded along the ways of perfection and holiness». When he celebrated he was seen marvellously absorbed in God and the profound piety of his soul could be read on his face. Before dying, with enthusiasm, with a surge of living faith, with indescribable emotion, he asked for and received the Viaticum, the great Consoler of the final moments of life. What do all these things tell us? That he was truly a man of God, «homo Dei».

Another love that vibrated strongly, most strongly, in the soul of Cardinal di Belmonte was for Mary Most Holy, Mother of God and our mother.

St. Anthony of Padua greeted the Virgin «Domina mea»; and our Cardinal, «Spes mea». This man of God was often seen with the Rosary in his hands and in the contemplation of the Mysteries of the Rosary found heavenly joy. In the last years of his life at Santa Marta, in the Vatican, when his strength was weakened, diminished, no longer able to devote himself to the apostolate, armed with pliers he prepared Rosaries to give away. To the persons to whom he offered them he used to say: «I give you this Rosary, recite it every day, Our Lady will protect you». With how much enthusiasm Don Gennaro spoke of Mary, of her beauty, of her patronage, of her mercy, is difficult to describe. To intimate persons he said one day: «In afflictions, in discouragement, when storms rage against us, let us call upon Our Lady and we shall surely experience how great is her patronage!». Beautiful ejaculatory prayers he raised to the Virgin and the name of the heavenly Queen sounded sweetly on his lips.

Relatives, familiar persons, have attested that Don Gennaro had a special devotion to Our Lady of Sorrows. Under the purple he wore the insignia of the Third Order of the Servants of Mary, which he took on 28 November 1916 in the Church of St. Marcellus in Rome.

In his room he had the image of Our Lady of Sorrows;

at her feet he often contemplated the martyrdom of Christ on Calvary and that of the Mother at the foot of the Cross. In the contemplation of these mysteries he was moved and perhaps suffered much.

Cardinal di Belmonte had devotion to various Saints and especially to Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus. He was the Ponens of the cause of sanctification of this Virgin, who was raised to the honors of the Altars in 1925. From the moment she was sanctified he raised to her special prayers and St. Thérèse, before being a Saint, obtained for him a notable grace.

The great-nephew Raimondo del Balzo told me one day: «In 1933 I was ill in a clinic in Rome; my Uncle the Cardinal visited me often and sometimes also heard my confession. In my sufferings he exhorted me to commend myself to St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus. She is powerful, he told me: he told me that while he was at Monte Mario in a little villa, he underwent there an operation on the bladder, from which the surgeon extracted eleven stones. Much time passed and the wound did not heal; he was in danger of gangrene. He had recourse with faith to Saint Thérèse, and one evening, when the pain raged most, before falling asleep, he commended himself to her and applied a relic of hers to the dressing of the wound and fell asleep. In the morning the attending doctor, to the greatest astonishment, found it healed. My Uncle told this episode, said Raimondo, with singular candor and since then I too began to have devotion to the Virgin of Lisieux».

From what I have narrated it is clear, it is manifest that Cardinal di Belmonte was truly «homo Dei».

During the occupation of Rome by German troops, Cardinal di Belmonte was forced to leave his beautiful, smiling residence of Monte Mario, moving to a small apartment in the Palace of the Holy Office, where he remained for a short time, since by special concession, in October 1944, he moved to Santa Marta, in Vatican City, together with his sister Anna.

This woman was his comfort, his confidante, the creature who had for him the greatest care and was pious, wholly the Lord's, the Angel of the house.

She died about a year before her brother.

I like here to go back a little in the narration of the departure of the distinguished Cardinal from Monte Mario.

I think that before leaving the beloved residence in which he had lived for about twenty years he must have felt a sense of sadness in his soul. That hill was the place of so many of his meditations, of so many elevations to God, of so many apostolic activities.

His villa has an interesting historical memory; in it a great part of the meetings concerning the Concordat between the Holy See and Italy were held. Taking part were His Eminence Cardinal Pietro Gasparri, Secretary of State of Pope Pius XI, Monsignor Borgoncini Duca, Substitute of the Secretariat of State of His Holiness, the lawyer Francesco Pacelli for the Vatican and the jurist State Counsellor Barone for the Italian Government.

Many beautiful memories, therefore, must have come to the mind of the venerable Cardinal in the act of leaving Monte Mario and, thinking perhaps that he would never return, from the depth of his heart he will have exclaimed: «Domine, fiat voluntas tua!».

At Santa Marta the spirit of the Cardinal day by day united itself more to God while his body slowly declined. Weakened in strength, he received the indult to celebrate seated, but he rarely made use of the privilege. With slow steps he walked only in the bedroom and in the study. Amid various pains never did words of complaint or impatience leave his lips; he suffered serenely, he made clear that in his heart were engraved the great words of Christ: «Blessed are they who suffer».

At the beginning of February 1948 he felt a severe renal insufficiency. The attending physician Prof. Filippo Rocchi visited him, and did not hide from the sick man's relatives the gravity of the case, counting, however, on the exceptional constitution of the Cardinal; Prof. Bonanome too, called in consultation, formulated the same diagnosis.

The most intense and affectionate care was lavished on the sick man; around him were his devoted secretary Mgr. Giovanni Battista Camoni, his nephew Carlo Maresca di Camerano, his great-nephews Prince of Belmonte Gioacchino Granito, Baron Gioacchino Malfatti di Montetretto, Raimondo del Balzo, Duke of Presenzano, and the religious nurses of the Conceptionist Order.

The Cardinal, as soon as he became aware of his poor state of health, asked with great insistence for the last Sacraments.

Throughout the whole illness he had received Holy Communion daily from Mgr. Camoni; Extreme Unction was administered to him by the Parish Priest of Vatican City, Fr. Fattorini, an Augustinian. With how much reverence he received the last Sacraments is difficult to describe.

During the illness, the Roman Pontiff Pius XII took such interest in him that several times he sent to the beloved Prince of the Church the comforting Apostolic Blessing through the Substitute of the Secretariat of State, His Excellency Monsignor Giovanni Battista Montini, now Archbishop of Milan, and Monsignor Carlo Grano, Head of Protocol.

The Pontiff having learned that the sick man's condition was worsening, without notice went in person to the very modest apartment occupied by the Cardinal in the Hospice of Santa Marta. The appearance of His Holiness, writes «L’OSSERVATORE ROMANO», in the humble monastic cell brought the sick man unspeakable joy and relief. The sick man expressed his gratitude to the Lord for having granted him so high and exceptional a seal upon his earthly pilgrimage and wished to reaffirm to the Successor of Peter, to the Angelic Pastor, whom he had always venerated with ineffable devotion, his fidelity. Words of fatherly comfort, of most heartfelt affection the Vicar of Christ addressed to Cardinal Granito and gave him, once more, the apostolic Blessing. Moved, he withdrew from his bedside. The dear visit cheered with admirable serenity the last days and the final hours of the just man, of the man of God.

On 15 February the sick man's condition became alarming; but during the night he had a little rest.

The powerful passion of the Cardinal, in all his long life, was the Holy Host, and this stronger passion tormented him on his deathbed.

At two o'clock on the day before his passing, he asked once more for the God of love, the Eucharistic King. He was satisfied. What he said to his Beloved in that last Communion only He knows who feeds among the white lilies, and the angels who attended him.

The colloquy was certainly intimate, arcane, transcendent!

The setting of the luminous Star draws near. The sick man, feeling sister death near, recited several times with those present the prayers for the dying, then abandoned himself with great and complete conformity to his Lord and to the heavenly Mother, whom he invoked in a subdued voice; and crossing his arms gently, softly, on his breast, with an angelic smile on his lip, he fell asleep in the kiss of the Lord. He died at 10 o'clock on 16 February 1948: a few weeks were lacking to the completion of his 97th year of life.

Cardinal di Belmonte is dead, zealous prince of the Holy Church, honor of the Sacred College, gigantic figure among the throng of ministers of the Sanctuary; he has vanished, it is true, from the stage of the world, yet his classic figure still shines luminously in the midst of Christendom. His spirit hovers and vibrates in the charm of his goodness, of his interior life, of his priestly zeal, in the radiating splendor of all his works of good.

Upon his tomb one could write the great words of Job: «There will arise for you towards evening a light like noonday, and when you think yourself destroyed you will rise like the morning star; buried, you will sleep in peace and many will address prayers to you».

Centuries will pass, dynasties will fall, nobility, human greatness, but Cardinal di Belmonte will not know oblivion; he will shine through the centuries like a star of the first magnitude in the sky of the Church of Christ.

At the hour of his passing there were present His Most Reverend Eminence Cardinal Raffaele Rossi, his Confessor Fr. Ottavio Marchetti S. J., the Secretary Monsignor Camoni and the aforementioned relatives and family members.

The illustrious Cardinal retained clarity of mind to the last moments of his life.

Monsignor Montini, Archbishop of Milan, wrote: «A moving fact I recall: Cardinal di Belmonte had me called before he died (I went on Sunday and he died on Monday).

He spoke to me with perfect lucidity of his imminent end, he recommended some things to me with a solicitude which made me see one last time the serene and noble goodness of his spirit».

H. E. Fra Carlo Maresca di Camerano, Bailiff, Grand Cross of Justice and Grand Prior of Naples and Sicily of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, writing to his cousin Raimondo del Balzo, said to him: «We followed closely the last part of the Cardinal's life and by tradition we had knowledge of the first. We were present together at his passing, which crowned his whole holy existence. In my long hospital career I have attended the death of hundreds of persons; the greater part of them were not in clarity of mind to understand the great moment that was approaching. Few, very few, did I see prepared and ready. None, really none, died in my presence like our dear Uncle. Do you remember the instructions given by him for the operations to be carried out after death: «the doors to be closed, the clothes to be prepared?» Everything he ordered with great presence of mind accompanied by his usual jesting tone of voice. The Uncle died as he lived, as a saint».

The sad news was immediately communicated to the Holy Father; then it spread rapidly in all circles, arousing everywhere the most heartfelt regret.

The blessed body was laid out in the Lying-in-state Chamber, set up in the Hall of Santa Marta.

At the death of Cardinal di Belmonte there were grandiose expressions of mourning. The blessed body was piously laid out in the spacious Hall of Santa Marta in Vatican City; four candles surrounded it: at the feet was placed the red hat. Further on were the prie-dieux for the very many persons who came to pay him the tribute of Christian suffrage; along the side walls four altars were arranged for the celebration of the Holy Masses, which were very many.

«L’OSSERVATORE ROMANO» described minutely all the expressions of mourning which the great Departed received.

The Organ of the Vatican wrote that the Prefect of Pontifical Ceremonies, Monsignor Enrico Dante, following the venerated dispositions of His Holiness, issued the special intimatio for the solemn funeral Papal Chapel, which took place on Thursday 19 February 1948 at 10.30 in the Vatican Basilica and precisely in the transept of Sts. Processus and Martinian.

His Most Reverend Eminence Cardinal Federico Tedeschini, Archpriest of the Patriarchal Vatican Basilica, pontificated the Requiem Mass.

At the end of the Divine Sacrifice the Roman Pontiff, Pius XII, who had so much affection and so much regard for the great Departed, imparted the absolution.

All the participants of the papal Chapels were invited.

The ceremony of the rogito and the closing of the coffin took place on Wednesday at 11 o'clock. In the afternoon, at 16 o'clock, the body was carried in private form to the Vatican Basilica and laid in the middle of the said transept.

The influx of high personages and of simple faithful to the body was uninterrupted.

All the Most Eminent Cardinals resident in Rome went to offer an affectionate demonstration of reverent homage and of suffrage to their most beloved Dean, who for fully eighteen years, with so much prestige, held the high office.

Moreover, other prelates of the Secretariat of State, the members of the Pontifical Antechamber, the Archbishops and Bishops; the Assessors and Secretaries of the Sacred Roman Congregations; the Superiors General of the Religious Orders followed one another uninterruptedly at Santa Marta.

Reverent and conspicuous was the last farewell of the Most Excellent Diplomatic Corps. The Most Excellent Relatives of His Holiness attended, all the ecclesiastical and lay dignitaries of the Pontifical Court, all the major exponents of the offices which depend on the Holy See.

Meanwhile a true plebiscite of universal regret takes shape, with very many telegrams of condolence.

To the Secretariat of State there came a personal dispatch from H. E. the Hon. Enrico de Nicola, President of the Italian Republic; for brevity I make no mention of so many others. Around the Cardinal's bier the participation of the Dioceses of Ostia and Albano was fervent. There went to Santa Marta Monsignor Giovanni Battista Trovalusci, formerly Vicar General of the Most Eminent Bishop for Albano, with Monsignor Giuseppe Stella, diocesan assistant of Catholic Action, and Father Carlo Moroni, Augustinian, Episcopal delegate of Ostia.

From the Diocese of Albano came moved telegrams of condolence from Parish Priests, from Mayors, from private groups. Significant were the acts of recognition from the circles of study, of science, of artists.

The news of the death of Cardinal di Belmonte, at once, by radio, spread through the world, causing in all who knew him mourning and sorrow. But especially it caused deep anguish in the souls of the religious men and women of whom he was Cardinal Protector.

How many of them at the announcement of his death burst into tears, how many moved ran to the feet of the holy altars to commend him to the clemency of God, how many Priests celebrated Holy Mass in suffrage for his blessed soul!

But how is it that there were so many expressions of mourning, of affection, of prayers for Cardinal di Belmonte?

He had so many expressions of mourning because he had the reputation of a Saint. A saint is the man who practizes the virtues of the faithful servants of God, who are especially united to Him by the gift of Faith. And who can adequately narrate the living, active Faith of Cardinal di Belmonte?

God stood at the top of his thoughts, he bore His Name engraved in great letters on his heart; in all that he did the most noble end of the glory of God always dominated.

The Supreme Being, the Creator of all things was his center, his heartbeat, his ideal, his treasure.

In a Pastoral written by him during the last world war, he affirmed: «The men who today make the world tremble under their war machines will pass away, but God remains for ever to test and reward, to cast down and raise up men, to make strike on the dial of history, which marks tremendous and dark hours, the last hour; which is always His hour, that of His triumph, because an hour of justice, of truth and of love».

His Faith in God was that of a Saint; perhaps the motto of the Poor Man of Assisi «Deus meus et omnia» often resounded on his lips.

And not only did Cardinal di Belmonte feel in his soul a most lively Faith for his God, but he felt also the virtue that consoles souls, which is Hope.

This virtue makes man superior to himself, making him love earthly things not at all, driving him continually towards heavenly ones. The quality of Hope is deduced from the quality of Faith. St. Bernard wrote: «Quantum quis credit tantum sperat». Christian Hope makes one suffer, makes one grieve, makes one weep for the ideal of the eternal joy which God has promised to those who serve and love Him. For this heavenly Hope Cardinal di Belmonte made himself voluntarily poor, suffered not a little in the Nunciature of Vienna; on his deathbed, amid bitter pains, he had a smile on his lip.

In his Pastoral letter «THE HOUR OF GOD» he wrote: «Let us revive our Hope in God who sees all, can do all, loves all, and let us have confidence in His power, in His goodness, in His love; our expectations will be realized in the measure in which we have hoped in Him».

Cardinal di Belmonte was the faithful friend of Christian Hope and I think that often, like the Seraphic Saint, from the depths of his soul he exclaimed: «So great is the good I look for that every pain is a delight to me».

Of the fire of charity which he felt for the Lord and for his neighbor we have spoken several times in these pages; I limit myself simply to saying that for Cardinal di Belmonte the purple was the tunic of love, of compassion, of altruism. With Charity, with this queen of the virtues, he governed over souls and over hearts, overcame hatreds and vengeances, triumphed serene over all the adversities of life. He was the lover of charity and brought comfort to the afflicted, the forsaken, the abandoned; in his heart the words of Christ vibrated strongly: «Beati misericordes» = blessed are the merciful.

The Catholic world was moved before the death of Cardinal di Belmonte, because it knew him as a most faithful servant of God, exemplary in piety, in doctrine, in government, endowed with incomparable virtue and wisdom.

It wept for him, because it saw a man set who was great in the true sense of the word in the field of holiness, of true social good, with a name linked to various important events in the history of the Church.

On 21 December 1941 the excellent Cardinal wrote a letter to Prof. Canon Onofrio Buonocore; in it are found these great words: «I give thanks to the Lord, who keeps my old age in a condition to be able to serve the Church». Buonocore comments thus on this expression: «There is a sentence in the letter which is a program of priestly life: to serve the Church! From the pen of an old man that expression is a watchword to young Priests in particular. To serve the Church as he served her, a young man of spotless habits, upright in the lay state, a priest kindled with every good daring, without excessive calculations either about life or about the wise use of riches, a faithful servant of the Pope in the most delicate mis-

sions, in the tangle of diplomacy, a dignified representative of the Pontiff in imposing situations, a Cardinal of firm purposes, at the side of his Lord in luminous hours as in dark ones, when at ninety and more years he still feels the pride of serving the Church. What a fine moral testament he leaves to those who will come after, that which was the program of a life without rest: to serve the Church!».

From these reflections it is clear, it is manifest, that the general expressions of mourning and of affection rendered to the great Departed are the seal of the splendor of his virtues, of his luminous holiness.

Cardinal Granito di Belmonte was born of a rich and noble family, inherited many properties, especially from his mother, Donna Francesca di Paola Pignatelli y Aymerich, an heiress, of Spanish origin.

Don Gennaro had possessions not only in Italy but also in Spain; he was rich, and that is why in his youth he undertook long journeys, and with the title of Count of Copertino lived brilliantly in society.

But from the moment he abandoned the world and put on the cassock, he consecrated his heart completely to God; and from then on riches had no value for him; he considered them as means of doing good to humanity.

The working of God's grace in his soul was grandiose!

He, I think, in order to come to the conclusion of detaching himself completely from earthly things, must have thought of blessed Christ, lord of heaven and earth, God Son of God, who for love of men willed to be born in a stable amid the greatest misery. He must have thought that Christ lived poor, always poor, and that one day He uttered this lament: «The foxes have their dens, the birds of the air their nests, but the Son of God has nowhere to lay his head».

He must have thought of the Almighty Martyr of Calvary who, amid a thousand sorrows, a thousand spasms, died in utter poverty, naked, on the bare cross.

To reach the resolve of stripping himself of everything, of giving, always giving, the marvellous verses in which Dante says that on Calvary Mary remained at the foot of the cross, while Lady Poverty climbed upon it and stood beside the dying Son, must have come to Don Gennaro's mind.

«Sì che, dove Maria rimase giuso

Ella con Cristo salse in su la Croce».

Here I wish to recall briefly how Don Gennaro disposed of his riches, how he became poor for Jesus Christ.

He was generous in alms to those struck by the earthquake of Casamicciola in 1883 and to the cholera victims and their families in Naples in 1884.

He spent a great deal of money to support and maintain, in its prestige, the Catholic newspaper «LA LIBERTÀ» in Naples.

He was most lavish towards the Sisters of St. Anne, in Naples and then in Rome, when they built the Church and the Generalate House on Via Merulana. At his own expense he caused Churches to rise from the foundations in the Diocese of Albano, and he often gave money for the needs of the Diocese of Ostia. He owned in Spain considerable property, and he donated it to the «Servants of the Sacred Heart» Sisters.

The munificent Cardinal encouraged the class of scholars. Shortly before he died, to give but one example, he had the joy of seeing published the learned volume by Alberto Galieti: «Contributi alla storia della Diocesi Suburbicaria di Albano Laziale».

The not inconsiderable costs of printing, «L’OSSERVATORE ROMANO» wrote, could be met thanks to the generosity of the Venerable Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, who counted among his cares that of favoring research that would serve to give ever more splendid honor to the two Dioceses entrusted to him by Divine mercy.

In his residences poverty always appeared dominant to visitors.

At Monte Mario, yes, it is true, he had a fine dwelling, but the bed, the study, the furnishings had an air of poverty. When he moved to the palace of the Holy Office, he settled there with his sister Anna and the secretary Mgr. Camoni in poor little rooms.

At Santa Marta, in Vatican City, he had a better lodging, but in the matter of poverty it did not differ from the preceding ones. In the last days of his life a pious Capuchin Father visited him; this Religious told his confreres that Cardinal Granito di Belmonte’s bed differed little from that of the Capuchins. — Sister Anna Romano, of the Daughters of St. Anne, present Superior of the House «Opera Pia Maria Grazia Barone» in Foggia, who for three months looked after the Cardinal’s sister, Anna, when she was gravely ill, told me one day: «The Cardinal’s house was like a Sanctuary, where there was frequent prayer and frequent talk of Christian virtues; the table was modest, frugal, democratic, it seemed like one of those of the first Christians; seated at it were: the Cardinal, the Secretary, the driver, the nurse, the servant and sometimes other intimate persons who came to visit him».

Poor, always poor, poor in everything, Don Gennaro. In his last testamentary dispositions, «L’OSSERVATORE ROMANO» wrote, dated 1 September 1947, he summed up his industrious priestly life thus: «Bishop, Cardinal, wholly devoted to the divine service».

«In the name of the Most Holy Trinity, of Most Holy Mary, of my Guardian Angel and of the Saints my Advocates and Protectors, in full possession of my mental faculties I write this my last will. With a transport of humility and love I lay my soul in the Most Holy Heart of Jesus Christ». There follow the dispositions concerning bequests to this or that religious institution, with the premise: «I declare that I leave no goods to take away with me».

He died in utter poverty. What was his tomb? Surely for Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, as a nobleman, as Count of Copertino, as a Prince of the Holy Roman Church, a rich tomb worthy of him could not be lacking. — A rumor spread, when he was gravely ill, that he would be buried in St. Peter’s or in the Church of the Capuchins of St. Lawrence of Brindisi, on Via Sicilia. They were rumors. The man of God lived poor and, before closing his eyes to the light of day, thought of resting in peace in a sepulchre of the poor. By his express wish, his body was laid in the tomb of the Capuchin Fathers at the Verano; there he rests in peace.

What is the tomb of the illustrious Purpurate, the precious gem of the Catholic Church, like?

Around the Basilica of St. Lawrence at the Verano, writes Father Giuseppe da Brà, Capuchin, there stood in ancient times numerous buildings furnished with towers, enclosed together with the Abbey and the Basilica by great crenellated walls. One of these towers, which rises at the foot of the Pincetto, is the present tomb of the Capuchins; it is old and large, but poor within, very poor.

Among so many religious who before the Altar promised God to be poor all their lives and who now rest in it, lies the great voluntary poor man, Cardinal Granito di Belmonte.

TRANSLATION. — Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte – Of noble Neapolitan family – Dean of the Sacred College of Cardinals – Most zealous Prelate of the Suburbicarian Diocese of Albano – Subsequently of Ostia – He was visited in his agony – With particular benevolence – By the Supreme Pontiff Pius XII – Who – By His August Presence – Wished to make more solemn for the Deceased – The funeral honors – In the Vatican Basilica – Here, according to his wishes – In the peace of the Lord – The Distinguished Purpurate rests – Beside those Capuchin Friars – Most dear to him – Whose cause he had long since been appointed to defend – By Order – Of His Holiness Benedict XV – Born in Naples on 10 April 1851 – After a long life – Adorned with unblemished virtues – Most piously he died – At the age of ninety-seven – On 16 February 1948.

The splendor of Cardinal Granito di Belmonte’s virtues is the reason for his true greatness, but he is great above all for the powerful passion he felt for holy poverty.

Riches never make a man great, but detachment from them, contempt for them.

Who would have written and spoken so much of Francis of Assisi had he not been a most virtuous man, a poor man? Who would have remembered his father, Pietro Bernardone, the miser, had he not had an immoderately prodigal son? Christ saw the whole excellence of poverty and therefore, on the mount of the Beatitudes, he exclaimed: «Beati pauperes».

Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte was born rich, lived poor, died poor and wished his body to rest in a sepulchre of poor religious.

The story of his life has something marvellous, something grand about it.

He passed among men and things with the lightning-flashes of the apostle, shone like a beacon amid the darkness, stood up like a wall of bronze to defend the rights of the Church; earthly things for his heart were nothing, were vanity.

Let us pray to the benign God that this Pilgrim of love, this resplendent gem of the Sacred College, this incomparable Laborer in Christ’s vineyard may be known, loved and imitated everywhere; only thus can a troubled society begin times of love and peace!

Before closing this chapter I wish to make my own the words that H. E. Mgr. Mario Palladino, Bishop of Caserta, spoke in a lecture on Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza, and which I apply to Cardinal di Belmonte: «May this moving spectacle of greatness, of heroism, of love; may the sufferings borne for the Church and for souls, the genius of pastoral government and a whole school of justice, prudence, fortitude, charity, goodness and zeal be at last recognized and approved by the Church».

I say to those who will read these pages: Let us pray and hope that God, all-wise, rewarder of his faithful servants, may grant glory also on this earth, for his greater glory, to the pious Cardinal di Belmonte, who passed among men poor, but as a vision of love, scattering rays of heavenly light on souls and hearts.

There are extant from Cardinal di Belmonte addresses to the Supreme Pontiff on the occasion of great solemnities, hundreds upon hundreds of letters sent to friends, in Italy and abroad. Five Pastoral Letters. In these writings his beautiful soul is always revealed, together with his attachment to Holy Mother Church. I publish the very beautiful address he delivered to the Holy Father on the eve of Christmas 1946, when a wave of anti-religion and vilification was wont to rise against the Vicar of Christ, and then some letters of his. Here is the address:

Most Blessed Father,

Thanks to the mercy of God, ever blessed, to whom I owe unending gratitude, I am granted this year also the high honor and the heartfelt satisfaction of becoming the humble interpreter of the good wishes of the Sacred College and of the Roman Prelature for Your Holiness, on the ever auspicious occasion of the Christmas and New Year Feasts.

And with affectionate, reverent devotion I present these good wishes to You in the light and fervor of a wealth of sentiments that burn in our hearts at this solemn moment, as we reflect on Your Apostolic deeds, on Your admirable industry, continued also in the year, none too happy, now drawing to its close.

My advanced age and many evident circumstances oblige me, alas, to forgo the customary retrospective survey, which would be so interesting and edifying; I cannot, however, omit the, if fleeting, mention of three facts of exceptional import, already won for the history of the Church; facts that shine like living constellations in the glorious sky of Your Pontificate, O Most Blessed Father, and that cast their light upon the future. I mean:

1st - The great Consistory of last February, which had such favorable resonance throughout the world and which greatly accentuated the catholicity of the Holy Roman Church;

2nd - The establishment of the Episcopal hierarchy in that immense Country which is China, rich in so many energies and promises for the religious future of its sturdy people, now judged ripe for the passage from the Mission regime to the Diocesan regime, under the guidance of its own Ordinary Bishops.

A tangible fruit this of the blood shed by the Martyrs of 1900, a chosen portion of whom was recently raised to the honor of the Altars.

3rd - The development of the providential and beneficent activity of the Pontifical Commission for Assistance, the true longa manus of the charity of the Pope, of the Common Father, which reaches wherever there is a sorrow to soothe, a tear to dry, a comfort to bestow, a victim to snatch from despair, from the snares of death.

Nor does the raging of rancor and hatred of certain modern and disguised persecutors serve to diminish the importance and efficacy of such weighty and reconstructive undertakings of the Catholic Church. On the contrary: even the most sorrowful and iniquitous trial at Zagreb, which brought so much pain and offense to Your heart, O Holy Father, has not served, nor does it serve, except to unmask such political currents, while it goes on gathering, together with the protests and execrations of every part of the civilized world, the warmest and most significant testimonies of filial affection, devotion and attention to Your Sacred Person. We wish, however, that from this venerable Assembly too there may go forth a cordial fraternal greeting, with full assurance of our solidarity, to the illustrious and innocent Archbishop of Zagreb, exemplary and heroic Pastor, struck by so unjust a condemnation.

In conclusion, I also wish to gather the echo of the hearts of all the devoted sons of the Sacred College and to raise to this August Throne our renewed thanks for the tireless magisterium of the word which You, Most Blessed Father, wisely continue from the Chair of Peter, the one Chair of Truth, of sure and unassailable doctrine. Your fatherly voice, indeed, is renewed often, seizing every propitious occasion to enlighten, admonish, comfort and gently guide. Would that all might profit by it, and particularly those who hold in their hands and are about to decide the fates of so many nations of the whole world! And would that they might be persuaded, at last, that a peace without true justice, a peace that would dispense with Christian doctrine and conscience, cannot be a just and lasting peace!

These wishes, together with Your particular intentions, O Most Blessed Father, we earnestly commend to the Divine Infant, Prince of peace, while we fervently beseech Him that, through the intercession of His and Our Mother Mary, refuge of sinners and conqueror of heresies, He may deign to pour out His mercies, His graces also upon our enemies, our persecutors, upon all these our straying brethren who, through the vulgar attacks and outrages of a shameless and sacrilegious press, have for some time been raging against Holy Mother Church and cruelly embittering the Heart of her Visible Head, the Sweet Christ on earth. May they too be converted and live! Et ipsi convertantur et vivant!

Holy Father «Ad multos annos». Bless us.

Cardinal di Belmonte, on his 90th year of life, received good wishes and congratulations from Most Eminent Cardinals, from Most Reverend Excellencies, Archbishops and Bishops, from Nobles, from relatives, from friends, from so many souls, so many hearts. — On this occasion the Roman Pontiff, Pius XII, sent him a message that is beautiful, sublime, sculptural, in which the figure of the Cardinal Dean stands forth resplendent in exceptional greatness.

TRANSLATION FROM THE LATIN

To Our Venerable Brother Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, Bishop of Ostia and of Albano, Cardinal of the H. Roman Church, Dean of the H. College and Prefect of the H. Congregation of Ceremonial.

PIUS XII POPE

Our Venerable Brother, health and Apostolic Blessing.

To complete one’s ninetieth year of age with such vigorous keenness of mind and such flourishing physical strength is a very rare thing and is certainly granted to very few. And indeed this Venerable Old Age is not only free of suffering and inertia, but industrious and ever intent on some task, such, that is, as was the liveliness of spirit in your earlier life. It is a most joyful thing for your admirers and chiefly for Us to look back and, with a pleasant mind, retrace so long a course of years adorned with so many merits and so many splendid praises.

In the flower of your youth, in Naples, your native city, there shone forth, in the sacred offices entrusted to you, singular piety and love for your neighbor. Your industrious virtue shone especially when, after distributing daily food to the people, you made yourself, with every effort and every device, a most ardent champion and guardian of Catholic liberty.

As time went on, because of the outstanding gifts of mind and heart with which you were adorned, five Roman Pontiffs did not hesitate to entrust to you weighty and honorable offices, as We Ourselves, through Our own offices, have well known, being the closest witnesses of your prudence and your ability.

Indeed, on behalf of this Apostolic See you either headed solemn and extraordinary Embassies in France, in Russia, in England, to the Belgians, or exercised assiduous activity in them.

After you were added to the College of Cardinals by Pius X, of h. m., Our Predecessor, you never ceased to labor with singular care and intelligence in the sacred Council of the Roman Curia for the advancement of the Catholic cause, and for more than ten years you have presided over the Congregation of Ceremonial.

Moreover, you happily fulfilled the office of Legate a latere of the Pontiff at Lourdes, at Orléans, at Palermo, presiding over the splendid rites.

The Faithful of Albano, to whom eleven years ago the sons of Ostia were also added, have experienced for more than twenty-five years your fatherly care and pastoral solicitude.

All of these, indeed, hold you in dear goodwill and veneration because you let slip no occasion to benefit either Flock.

We, then, anticipating the chorus of those who congratulate you, wish you the happiest and most joyful things; we pray God with insistent prayer that He may preserve for a long time and protect this old age and graciously enrich the pastoral office with abundant fruits.

That the faithful may draw from your auspicious anniversary a greater abundance of fruits, We grant you of Our own accord that in both dioceses, on the day that shall please you, after Mass celebrated in the Pontifical rite, you may bless in Our Name and by Our Authority the people present, imparting to them the plenary indulgence, to be gained according to the dispositions of the Church.

Moreover, may Our Apostolic Blessing, which We lovingly impart in the Lord to you, Our Venerable Brother, to all the Clergy and all the people of the two dioceses, and likewise to your relatives, your friends and the associates of your labors, be for you a conciliator of heavenly graces and a witness of Our particular goodwill.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, on 3 April 1941, the third year of our Pontificate.

PIUS PP. XII

He writes to the Most Rev. Fr. Raphael, Postulator of the Capuchin Fathers, asking him to gather information concerning the Capuchin Nun Sr. Maria Chiara of St. Francis, in whom He sees the stuff of a Saint.

Rome, 31 July 1933.

Most Rev. Fr. Raphael of Valfenera, Postulator General.

In the Community of the Capuchin Nuns of Via Aurelia Antica, at the beginning of this year, there died the Religious Maria Chiara of St. Francis (in the world Countess Guido Baldina Knefstein), the stuff of a Saint, very simple and without outward show.

The Abbess rightly thought it well to gather various items of news about the deceased, which drew the attention of the Most Rev. Father General and also my own, as their Protector. You should acquaint yourself with them in order to judge whether it is not the case to collect material that later might no longer be found for want of witnesses.

I believe it my duty to report the above to you, with the request that you take it in hand, and I am convinced you will judge that there is no time to lose.

If you think of visiting that Community, I could one day come to fetch you, and the information you judge necessary could be gathered directly.

If the Most Rev. Fr. General has not given you the information transmitted by the Mother Abbess, you may take a preliminary look at what I have, and thus you would go to the place already partly informed.

I greet you.

Most devotedly yours,

† G. CARD. GRANITO DI BELMONTE

He thanks His Excellency Monsignor Marinoni for the volume he sent him, «PIONEERS OF FAITH AND CIVILIZATION IN ERITREA», and expresses his admiration for the Missionary Spirit of the Capuchin Fathers.

Rome, 10 June 1938.

To His Most Reverend Excellency Mgr. Giancrisostomo Luigi Marinoni, Apostolic Vicar of Eritrea. — Asmara.

The gift that Your Excellency makes me of the interesting work «PIONEERS OF FAITH AND CIVILIZATION IN ERITREA» by Fr. Ezechia of Iseo has reached me.

Such a gift is most dear to me, because it comes from Your Most Rev. Excellency, and because, as Protector of the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin, I cannot but rejoice to find, in the enumeration of the historical facts recorded in the volume, an affirmation of the solid missionary spirit by which your Order lives, and an account of the individuals who most distinguished themselves in Eritrea.

I have written these lines in the very days in which I presided over the General Chapter of Your Order, where I had occasion to recognize the missionary spirit through the reports of the various Very Rev. Fathers Provincial, a spirit which it is dear to me today to praise in the Capuchins of Eritrea.

A page of Fr. Ezechia’s work interests me also very closely, and it is where he speaks of the Daughters of St. Anne, whose Protector I am also, and I have the joy of having been concerned, together with their venerated Foundress, Rosa Gattorno, in Naples, with the departure of the very first Daughters of St. Anne, who set out for Eritrea in 1886.

These Sisters too have made themselves deserving of that Mission, to the point that today they have in Eritrea one of the most flourishing Provinces of the Institute, with hundreds of religious.

A word of praise and satisfaction from me go to Fr. Ezechia of Iseo, author of the book indicated above.

I renew to Your Most Rev. Excellency my homage and thanks and, commending myself to your prayers, I remain:

† G. CARD. GRANITO DI BELMONTE

The Hon. Raffaele Pio Petrilli, now President of the Council of State, and his wife, the Noble Lady Maria Del Balzo, lost in 1940 a most virtuous daughter, Enrichetta, aged about thirteen and a half. The writer assisted her in her hard illness. As soon as the Cardinal learned the sorrowful news of her death, he wrote to the father this brief, consoling letter.

Rome, 10 March 1940.

Dearest Pio,

To you and to Maria I send, also in the name of Anna, affectionate condolences!

I have prayed for the dear and blessed soul! But I do not hide that I prayed more for you, the parents, than for that dear creature vanished from the earth. Enrichetta is now your Guardian Angel!

As good Christians you will certainly have conformed to the holy will of God! May your natural grief be an increase of glory for your beloved and virtuous daughter.

I bless you,

your most affectionate Uncle

† G. CARD. GRANITO DI BELMONTE

At Christmastide the Cardinal returned the good wishes of the Most Rev. Canon Onofrio Buonocore. He wrote:

Rome, 21 December 1941.

Most Rev. Canon,

With gratitude I thank you and your brother for the good wishes you had the kindness to send me for the Christmas season and the new year.

From my heart I pray God to repay you in blessings what you wish for me.

Every moment that passes I give thanks to the Lord, who keeps my old age in a condition to be able to serve the Church.

With distinguished greetings to you and to your brother, I remain:

† G. CARD. GRANITO DI BELMONTE

He informs Cardinal Nicola Canali of the work he has done with the Holy Father Pius XII so that the cause of the Holy Pontiff Pius X might be hastened.

Rome, 23 February 1942.

Most Eminent Cardinal NICOLA CANALI,

VATICAN CITY

In the audience that His Holiness granted me on Thursday the 19th inst. I dealt with the cause of the Holy memory of Pius X.

His Holiness showed himself in part already informed, and told me that he would willingly have recommended to the Most Eminent Cardinal Prefect of Rites to hasten the proceedings, but that he did not think the procedure required in such cases could be set aside; all the more since the cause was behind, not having yet been introduced.

I showed the letter of the Most Rev. Father General: he wished to keep it. The other writings of the Father General I did not show, and here I return them to Your Eminence.

Should I be informed of further measures, it will be my care to report them to Your Eminence, whose hands I humbly kiss.

† G. CARD. GRANITO PIGNATELLI DI BELMONTE

He thanks H. E. Monsignor Carinci for the gift of the Acts relating to the Canonization of the Saints: M. E. Pelletier and Gemma Galgani, of whose Cause He was Relator.

Rome, 2 June 1942.

H. E. Most Rev. Mgr. Alfonso Carinci, Secretary of the H. C. of Rites

ROME

To the tireless and exemplary Secretary of the H. C. of Rites I send many thanks for the new gift he makes me of the «Acta Canonizationis» of the Saints: Mary Euphrasia Pelletier and Gemma Galgani.

Excellency, this time the gift is all the more welcome, because it concerns dear Gemma Galgani, of whose Cause I was Relator.

I cannot understand how Your Excellency finds time to attend to these extraordinary labors, while the ordinary work of the H. C. of Rites is uninterrupted.

I explain it all by the special helps that Your Excellency receives from God, and which you know how to trade with, returning to God a hundredfold!

Again I thank you and with homage believe me yours:

† G. CARD. GRANITO PIGNATELLI DI BELMONTE

Baroness Adelaide von Gebstiel – Director General of the Pont. Association of Catholic Ladies for the Missions.

Friederichstrasse 261 MUNICH (Germany)

With Fr. G. we are always concerned with the Pontifical Association. — The parchment listing all the works and prayers offered on the occasion of His Episcopal Jubilee has been presented to the Holy Father.

Most Illustrious Sir,

I have considered your affectionate request concerning the lamented Uncle, Most Eminent Cardinal Gennaro Pignatelli di Belmonte. During the many years of his Protectorate over our Institute of the Little Brothers of Mary, how many signs of exquisite kindness he showed us! A counsel of his was a command, a wish of his was at once fulfilled, a favor of his showed the exuberance of his great heart.

On the occasion of his name day, 19 September, I used to accompany my good wishes and those of the Superior General with a basket of fruit. Once I did not manage to find what I needed and His Eminence, pleased, replied to me in French, which he spoke and wrote fluently: «Tant mieux, comme cela vous n’avez point fait de péché…».

He presided several times at the First Communions of the pupils of our College of St. Leo the Great. We remember the solemnity of the ceremonies and the simple but effective words addressed to the first communicants.

It was an honor for us to visit him in his fine residence on Monte Mario, as also in that of St. Martha in the Vatican; he always received us with great affability.

In the last years of his long life he was very weak; he could not stop thanking the Holy Father, who allowed him to celebrate seated.

As Cardinal Ponens of our Causes of Beatification, he lost no occasion to recommend them to the officials of the H. C. of Rites, especially that of the Ven. Founder.

Great kindness, exquisite courtesy, prudent and weighed counsel, he showed in his words. During a visit paid him by the Superior General and the Procurator General, he asked the Superior, half in earnest, half in jest: «Etes-vous content de ce Monsieur?…»

Every time I had occasion to meet the Most Eminent Cardinal GENNARO GRANITO PIGNATELLI DI BELMONTE I carried away that intimate and sweet impression which radiates from men of God, reflecting outwardly and diffusing a virtue of serenity and goodness.

Most Excellent Duke del Balzo,

I can tell you little of the life and habits of the lamented and venerated Card. Granito di Belmonte, because I had only weekly contacts with Him during my time as Vicar of the Diocese of Albano. Yet that was enough for me to judge and appreciate Him as He truly was, a holy Bishop, of profound interior life and proven wisdom in government. Of firm character, but not hard, he always had in his pastoral ministry the glory of God and the good of souls before his eyes; prudent and discreet, he deliberately shunned every hasty judgment of persons and events, and I never heard from his lips a single word that offended charity. Even in the face of great bitterness his bearing was dignified, as of a person in perfect command of himself. He was nobly generous, but his generosity aimed more at works than at persons, for which our Diocese owes Him the fine Churches and Rectories of Ciampino, Cecchina and Campoleone, the partial restoration of the Bishop’s Palace with its magnificent archive and various subsidiary foundations for the Clergy.

This, in sum, is what I can tell you as my judgment on the lamented Card. di Belmonte.

With most deferential respects.

Most Excellent Duke,

very glad to learn, from yours of the 9th inst., that Father Ilario of Teano, of the Capuchins, is about to complete the drafting of the biography of the Venerable and lamented Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, who was your Uncle. I was told of him, moreover, by all who knew him well, of his constant life of prayer, of recollection, of mortified poverty, of most generous and edifying charity.

The Handmaids of the Sacred Heart, who had him for so many years in circumstances such that they could know him well and follow him in his daily and luminous existence, related to me moving episodes about him, in which there always shone, together with his full dedication to the Church and to the Roman Pontiff, the apostolic zeal of his sacred ministry and the vivacity of his episcopal initiatives.

Most kind Duke,

I have always nourished the highest esteem, indeed the deepest veneration, for Card. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte. See, the fidelity with which he met the demands of his rank and of the charges entrusted to Him, the exquisiteness of his manners, derived not so much from the nobility of his house as from his generous and amiable nature, made of Him an exemplary prelate.

Almost a centenarian, he died rich in merits, leaving in all who knew him the most grateful and edifying memory.

It is remarkable that he, a conspicuous example of late vocation, succeeded in being a model priest and bishop, although he had not had in his early youth an adequate ecclesiastical formation.

Cher Monsieur le Duc,

J’ai bien reçu votre aimable lettre du 11 Novembre m’annonçant que le R. P. Ilario da Teano, O. F. M. C., prépare une biografie du Grand et Inoubliable Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, votre oncle; et je suis heureux de répondre à votre désir en vous faisant part du souvenir que je garde de cet illustre disparu que j’ai bien connu, et auquel me liait une longue et sincère amitié.

Dans la vie exemplaire de ce vénérable vieillard presque centenaire ce qui frappait de prime abord, c’était la lucidité de son intelligence et la fraîcheur de ses forces physiques: ce qui lui a permis de s’acquitter jusqu’à la fin de ses jours, des devoirs de sa haute dignité.

Je le vois encore, débordant de santé, et malgré ses 97 ans, vaquer normalement à ses occupations journalières, préparer méticuleusement les réunions cardinalices et consulter personnellement livres et documents relatifs aux questions de la S. C. des Rites.

Pleine de foi, sa vie était réglée par le rythme de pratiques quotidiennes de la piété et une dévotion particulière à la Sainte Vierge qui se traduisait par la récitation journalière du Rosaire.

Son affabilité devenue populaire, était l’un des aspects saillants de sa vraie humilité. Dans les modestes appartements qu’il occupait, il se révélait à ses différents visiteurs, le pasteur sage et surnaturel, et le diplomate fin et expert, que l’âge n’empêchait pas de traiter avec pondération et maîtrise des langues, les sujets divers d’actualité.

Aux fastes d’un cardinalat long, fécond et glorieux ce Prince magnifique — son testament en est la preuve — joignait une pauvreté personnelle extrême, pour avoir donné tout aux pauvres.

Par l’ardeur de son noble coeur, ce digne doyen du S. Collège, était un vrai modèle dans le respect et la défense des droits de l’Eglise, du Pontificat et de Dieu. Bref, je puis me résumer en disant: dans le Prince et le Cardinal, on voyait surtout, le prêtre laborieux, pieux, humble et charitable.

En vous bénissant de tout coeur, ainsi que l’auteur, le R. P. Ilario de Teano, je vous prie d’agréer, cher Monsieur le Duc, l’expression de mes sentiments affectueusement dévoués en N. S.

† J. G. CARDINAL TAPPOUNI

Beirut (Lebanon), 2 December 1955.

Dear Duke,

I have received Your kind letter of 11 November, in which you inform me that Rev. Fr. Ilario of Teano, O.F.M. Cap., is preparing a biography of the great and unforgettable Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, your Uncle, and I am happy to respond to your wish by sharing with you the memory I keep of this illustrious departed one, whom I knew well and to whom I was bound by a long and sincere friendship.

In the exemplary life of this venerable old man, almost a centenarian, what struck one first was the lucidity of his intelligence and the freshness of his physical strength, which allowed him to attend to the duties of his high dignity until the end of his days.

I still see him, full of health, despite his 97 years, going normally about his daily occupations, meticulously preparing the Cardinalitial meetings and personally consulting books and documents concerning the questions of the H. C. of Rites.

Full of faith, his life was governed by the rhythm of daily practices of piety and by a particular devotion to the Most Holy Virgin, which found expression in the daily recitation of the Rosary.

His affability, which had become proverbial, was one of the salient aspects of his true humility. In the modest apartment he occupied, he revealed himself to his various visitors as the wise and pious pastor, the fine and expert diplomat, whom age did not prevent from treating with balance and command of languages the diverse subjects of the day.

To the splendors of a long, fruitful and glorious cardinalate this magnificent Prince — his testament is the proof — added an extreme personal poverty, having given everything to the poor.

By the ardor of his noble heart this worthy Dean of the H. College was a true model in respect for and defense of the rights of the Church, of the Pontificate and of God.

In brief, I may sum up by saying: In the Prince and the Cardinal one saw above all the industrious, pious, humble and charitable Priest.

Blessing you with all my heart, as also the Author, Fr. Ilario of Teano, I beg you to accept, dear Duke, the expression of my affectionately devoted sentiments in O. L.

† IGNATIUS GABR. CARD. TAPPOUNI

Most kind Duke,

I heard of Card. Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte from childhood, in the family, and especially from my great-uncle Mgr. Ettore Sanfelice di Acquavella, Abbot Treasurer of the Chapel of the Treasure of St. Januarius in Naples.

The youth of the lamented Cardinal, his late vocation, the pioneering work which, as soon as he was ordained Priest, he carried out in Naples under the impulse of Card. Guglielmo Sanfelice di Acquavella and his subsequent brilliant «curriculum vitae» were familiar to me.1

The deepest impression, however, I received when I had the joy of knowing him personally, as a student of the Pontifical Roman Seminary and then in my frequent visits to Him, as a Priest.

Deeply attached to his city and his diocese, he asked for news of it with interest and showed for Naples and for its Clergy the liveliest love.

In dealing with him one saw that He strove to make his greatness disappear: the patrician vanished, the fine diplomat, the Cardinal Dean, and a Father spoke with the most natural simplicity and with the shrewd and good-natured directness of the Neapolitan gentleman. But whoever knew the struggles and bitterness he had had to accept on his way, whoever knew, even in the smallest part, what courage and what fortitude he had shown in his life, on the most varied and delicate occasions, remained amazed before that manner so free of haughtiness and so full of human warmth.

As he followed precisely and tenaciously all the duties of his very high office in the affairs of the Church, so with the same tenacity and with utmost kindness he took an interest in his even lesser charges.

I have seen long letters of his — in that fine clear round hand of his — to Superiors General of religious Institutes of which he was «Protector», in which he concerned himself even with individual cases, gave advice, went down to the smallest particulars, as if he had nothing else to do in his busy day.

It would also be interesting to collect the text of those brief but most dense and sculptural addresses with which each year, in his capacity as Dean, he presented to the H. Father the good wishes of the H. College. One would thus have before one’s eyes the history of the Church of these latter times as though filtered through his alert spirit, his profound feeling, his devotion to the Church and to the Pope.

In the last years, his appearance at the solemn papal functions was like a vision of other times, for in his venerable figure, which was only beginning to bend under the weight of his very many years, a very great heart throbbed and there was condensed the history of the Church of these latter times and the memory of the life, of the Neapolitan society of the nineteenth century.

He died poor: and this too was an index of his Christian life and of perfection, and his passing closed a cycle of time, definitively. His memory speaks even today, and is regret, and is warning, and is hope.

MGR. VITTORIO LONGO

Titular Bishop of Lorima and Auxiliary

of the Most Eminent Card. Archbp. of Naples

Capua, 9 May 1956.

Excellency,

I hasten to reply to Yours, particularly grateful for the gift you make me, giving me the occasion to express a thought of mine on a great Soul whom I had the good fortune to know as Priest and as Bishop, enjoying, without any merit of mine, the confiding goodwill and the comforting encouragement which he always granted me, ample and fatherly.

Of Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, most select Prince of the Church, ornament of the H. College, of which he was the most worthy Dean, Man of Curia and of Government, good, energetic and constructive Shepherd, one perceived at once at the first meeting the exceptional spiritual wealth, in which the highest virtues were nourished, and evident was its radiation in life upon souls.

The profound reflections — which at times took the form of genial remarks — that sprang from His great priestly heart remain alive in my memory, and time has made them more illuminating.

In Cardinal Granito Pignatelli, noble by birth, there shone the spirit of humility, of simplicity, of docility, which did not dim but rather adorned and made more resplendent the native nobility of the Saints, which draws and is enlightened precisely and only from humility and simplicity: «Quicumque humiliaverit se sicut parvulos iste, hic major est in regno coelorum». (Mt. 18:4).

In my meetings with the pious Cardinal what struck me most, and what my filial and venerating admiration increased, was the indifference to the things of the earth, that is, the full, absolute, evangelical detachment. He felt and practized the principle of St. Ignatius: «Necesse est nos facere indifferentes».

I recall with moved heart a significant episode that gives particular relief to the spirit of detachment of the Most Eminent Prince. To me, who with filial confidence pointed out to him what he would do if, having deprived himself of everything, God were to grant him a long life, he replied with these luminous words: «I want to ensure that nothing keeps me attached to the earth». And nothing, indeed, held Him back, and only in his flaming heart did the love of God reign.

It is with ardent faith that I raise the prayer to the Most High that He grant that the Most Eminent and Venerated Uncle of yours, vision of a beautiful and great soul, who served the Church with fidelity and love, radiating upon souls the odor Christi in the effluvium of his sublime virtues, now certainly glorious in Heaven, be glorified also on earth.

Accept, Excellency, the expression of my grateful and devoted spirit, as with outpouring fatherhood I bless You and Your family.

Devotedly in the Lord

† SALVATORE BACCARINI

Archbishop of Capua

Milan, 6 July 1956.

Most Noble Sir,

I am much obliged to You for Your most courteous good wishes; please accept in return my most sincere wishes for every good, in the Lord.

I am also flattered by the request You make me regarding my memory of the ever-lamented Most Eminent Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte. I do indeed keep of Him a memory full of veneration and esteem; but I should not know how to document it with particular reminiscences and adequate judgment.

I did not have many dealings with his venerated person. Those offered me by reasons of office always gave me the grateful and edifying impression of a very noble, grave and affable, humble and pious spirit. I remember him as a person of great balance, most devoted to the Pope and to the Church, wholly pervaded by the lofty awareness of his high ecclesiastical function, sustained with wisdom and dignity, with exemplary spirituality.

One moving fact I recall: he had me called before he died (I went, if I am not mistaken, on the Sunday, and he died on the Monday). He spoke to me with perfect lucidity of his imminent end; he commended some things to me, with a concern that let me see one last time the serene and noble goodness of his spirit.

He who could tell everything about him would have been Mgr. Camoni, dear and well known to You.

With particular respect, Yours devotedly in Christ.

† GB. MONTINI

Archbishop of Milan

Rome, 31 July 1956.

Most Ill. Doctor,

I have received Yours of the 21st inst. and applaud the initiative of Father Ilario of Teano, who wishes to compose the biography of a Man who, in a long life wholly spent in the service of the Church, so greatly honored both her and Italy.

During the years 1943–48, Card. Granito di Belmonte, your Uncle, wished to honor me with His affectionate friendship, and during His illness and afterwards I had the good fortune to spend long hours with Him in an exceptionally pleasant conversation, given His great intelligence, which remained most lucid to the last moments, his extraordinary and perfect memory, and his deep and good-natured wit.

I think Father Ilario may have frequent occasion to come to Rome, for archive research or other matters, and I should be very glad to meet him. I could show him some notes which, however schematic, may have a certain biographical value, also because written under the impression of the moment, and in conversation various memories and anecdotes may surface in my mind.

Most glad if I can be of even the slightest usefulness in recalling the figure of the Great Departed, I beg you, Doctor, to accept my most respectful greetings.

DR. SAMUELE SCHAERF

Physician - Surgeon

GRAND PRIORY OF NAPLES AND SICILY

OF THE SOVEREIGN ORDER OF MALTA

The Grand Prior

Naples, 30 July 1956.

Dear Raimondo,

For some time I have tried to call to mind some salient fact of the life of our beloved uncle, Cardinal Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, but without succeeding. My relations with him were marked by the utmost devotion that I had for him and by his cordiality towards me.

I was his guest the first time when he took lodgings in Corso d’Italia, newly raised to the purple. Later I enjoyed his hospitality in the house on Monte Mario.

My stay with him was always very brief and I spent most of the time with Aunt Anna.

We saw each other at table, and afterwards I would watch the tending of his canaries. This operation lasted over half an hour and was performed by him alone.

All his actions were carried out in a regular manner. — When I was his guest in Corso d’Italia, I had a room adjacent to his bedroom. Every morning, at the same hour, I heard a noise on the wall common to the two rooms. I learned afterwards that it was the click of the light switch. This noise preceded by one minute the sound of a pendulum clock. I say this to indicate the meticulousness of all his actions. The same happened at lunch or dinner time. He was never a single minute late or early.

I held him, in his simplicity, to be a true Saint, and the proof we had in attending his last days and moments.

His placid passage from this life to the other took place, as you yourself will have been able to observe, with the utmost tranquillity, as if it were a matter of a habitual act.

From the whole I always judged him a Saint, but I could not specify the motive of this conviction of mine, since every act of his, every word of his, was so simple and natural that it would have been strange had they not been so. I cannot tell you anything else of him that you do not know.

Cordial greetings from your affectionate

CARLO MARESCA

Asmara, 15 October 1956.

Most Excellent Duke,

with a delay, which you will forgive me since it is not due to negligence, I send you a letter addressed to me by the lamented Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte (see p. 114). It constitutes, in my modest opinion, a most eloquent document of the cordial interest with which the lamented and venerated Cardinal followed the missionary activity of our Order and of the satisfaction with which he recalled its contribution to the Mission of Eritrea.

All my confreres, and I myself personally, have always admired the lively and active participation of our most beloved Protector in all the events and problems of the Order, as if they concerned not only His office, but His very person, the innermost depths of His most sensitive soul. For this fatherhood of affection and of works, it seems to me that in the Card. Protector I find one of our most eminent confreres and superiors.

I believe that this sentiment of mine has been shared by all those who had occasion to deal with your venerated uncle.

Accept my sentiments of esteem and homage, as I am glad to profess myself, of Your Ill. Lordship,

Apostolic Vicar

Molfetta, 24 January 1957.

Dearest Confrere,

Your kind letter has reached me, in which you announce that the biography of your late uncle, Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, will shortly be published.

This news has filled my soul with joy, for I see at last fulfilled a wish that I expressed to you about two years ago.

The holy and blessed memory of the illustrious Purpurate, through the biographical notes, will live among posterity, and all those who read them, I hope, will strive to live as He lived, according to the heart of God.

How many lives of men are printed that in society did more harm than good, they ought not to be read, because they could cause spiritual disorders in souls.

Poor humanity needs to know men in the true sense of the word, great, lovers of duty and, above all, of God and his children. Such was Cardinal Granito.

He, a most luminous star in the sky of the Church, because by his heroic virtues he spread supernatural light among the peoples. Your uncle is for me a true genius, not in the arts and sciences, but in the field of the most flourishing charity.

How many afflicted he consoled, how many sorrows he soothed, how many works of good he left behind him!

From a deep sentiment of altruism he died poor and for this characteristic note of his heart he has been and will always be blessed.

I also rejoice at the publication of this biography because I see exalted the humble and pious Priest, luster and ornament of our Hierosolymitan Militia, since, as you well know, he was Bailiff Grand Prior of Rome.

I wish the book written by the excellent Father Ilario of Teano the very widest circulation, in the hope that many souls thirsting for good will find in it a school of light, of piety, of Christian perfection.

Accept, dearest Confrere, my cordial greetings and believe me always Yours

affectionately in Christ

MICHELANGELO TURILLO

All these distinguished persons with one voice have affirmed that CARDINAL DI BELMONTE is, as I have defined him in Chap. XII of this little volume: «Homo Dei»

The reasons that have led me to write this book are various; I mention here the principal ones.

In publishing it I have sought to please my dearest friend, Raimondo del Balzo, Duke of Presenzano, who in Rome with so much interest begged me to compile it.

I do not hide that it has cost me some sacrifice, because there are no biographers of the late Cardinal Dean.

All the memories, the most salient episodes of a life, as I have already said, I came to know through reviews, pamphlets, newspapers, unpublished manuscripts. I also had an excellent contribution of documentation from trustworthy persons who knew the Cardinal.

Whether I have pleased the Duke of Presenzano I do not know.

Likewise I do not know whether this book will be read with pleasure: the readers will say. I am almost certain, however, that the readers will praise my good will in making known a Bishop eminently humble, eminently poor, eminently pious, who lived on this earth of tears and blood, singing hymns of love to God and neighbor.

I have written of the distinguished Purpurate out of a sense of gratitude. I was never an acquaintance of his. I saw him once, in June 1938, in the Capuchin Friary on Via Boncompagni in Rome, when the Most Reverend Fr. Donato of Welle was elected Minister General. He came to preside over the Chapter. On that occasion I had the great joy of looking at him attentively, of kissing his Sacred Ring and of receiving his fatherly blessing.

My sense of gratitude arises from the great good that He did to my Order.

Searching in the library of the Capuchins on Via Sicilia in Rome for news of Him in «ANALECTA ORDINIS FRATRUM MINORUM CAPPUCCINORUM», I found described at so many points his solicitous action for the good, for the prosperity of the Order to which I belong, of which He was for thirty-three years Cardinal Protector.

In Rome I approached elderly, venerable Capuchins, not excluding the Most Rev. Fr. Benigno of Sant’Ilario, a Milanese, Minister General of the Order; I asked them for news and opinions of Cardinal di Belmonte, and an imposing chorus of praise came from their lips for so Eminent a Shepherd; all affirmed frankly that he was a true blessing of the Lord for the family of the Friars Minor Capuchin. He did great good to my Order and therefore deserves gratitude.

As results from these pages, Cardinal Granito was a true greatness, a true glory of the Catholic Church, because he served her with fidelity, made her known and respected. He loved his visible Head, the Roman Pontiff, with ineffable love; he saw in the Pope blessed Christ, Him who faced on Calvary a fearful martyrdom to give the Church supernatural life.

Cardinal di Belmonte shone like a luminous beacon amid the shadows of his century; he passed among the peoples adorned with gleams of resplendent light. To hand down to posterity, then, the merits of this pioneer of the Faith of Christ, who fought the holiest battles, is certainly a fine thing, pleasing to God and to men of good will.

Had I not written, perhaps the memory of his sacrifices, of his zeal, of his apostolate, of his heroic virtues would have faded. His gigantic figure, this modest work will not let be forgotten.

In writing the biography of Cardinal di Belmonte I set myself to give a valid contribution to the good press. Today a great part of the good press has strayed from its noble mission, that is, to make known the good in its varied fields.

The voices of such press often drive to great moral and social disorders. Society needs to know honest men who have practized true philanthropy, who have passed as visions of purest love in the midst of the masses.

One of these is without doubt Cardinal di Belmonte. Readers will find in his life a chair resplendent with light, goodness and charity without bounds. This luminous chair I wished to make known to readers.

In the present pilgrimage the groaning children of Eve are often visited by a whirlwind of physical and moral ills.

How many illnesses, how many afflictions, how many struggles, how many disillusionments they face in this life rightly called: «Vale of tears».

Most true are the great words of Job: «Man living a short time on this earth is filled with many miseries». = «Homo brevi vivens tempore repletur multis miseriis».

Amid so many afflictions, every man feels the need of supernatural help and, if so, why not ask it of God through the intercession of the late Cardinal Dean?

He lived as a Just man and died as a Just man. One would need flashes of genius to describe with how much sweetness, with how much resignation, with how much Faith he fell asleep in the kiss of the Lord.

And that God whom He so loved and so glorified, at the hour of passage from time to eternity was certainly close to him, and must have said to him: «Euge Serve bone et fidelis intra in gaudium Domini tui».

Who could ever, even remotely, doubt that Cardinal di Belmonte enjoys the beatific vision of God? Let us pray to him with a surge of heartfelt affection that he pray to God for all our needs and those of all poor humanity. And if through his supplications to the Almighty the lights of grace come down from Heaven upon poor mortals, he will pass blessed through the generations, and so the aims of this modest book will be truly great.
